news.title: UK 'Conservative' Party Leader Says Trump Deserved to Lose Midterms, Decries 'Dirty' Style of Politics
news.text:
The leader of the so-called Conservative Party, Kemi Badenoch, said U.S. President Donald Trump deserved to lose in the recent midterm elections and that she wouldn’t have minded if he had also lost to Democrat Kamala Harris in the 2024 election.

In an interview with the left-wing Independent news site, Tory leader Kemi Badenoch claimed that the recent midterm losses for Republicans in the United States were a result of “entirely self-inflicted” wounds by President Donald Trump. Badenoch said that while the war in Iran — which she supported — played a role, she also took aim at the U.S. leader’s “dirty” style of politics and even accused him of pursuing an agenda contrary to conservative values.

“He came in with this extraordinary coalition, you know, Latinos; he had more black voters than any other Republican, and what’s the first thing that he does? Tariffs. And then talking about Greenland and Canada, and I think a lot of people were wondering, what are you doing? Tariffs are bad for the cost of living. They’re not good,” she asserted.

The Tory party leader claimed that protectionism and America First policies were “not what conservatives do”, arguing that he should have continued the “free market” neo-liberal adherence to global trade, which hollowed out America’s manufacturing base as corporations sought cheaper labour in Asia and elsewhere.

“He has not been acting in the way that I would consider conservative,” she declared.

Badenoch also took particular aim at President Trump’s personality, saying that while she found him “very charming in person”, she did not approve of the “way he talks” about opponents.

“It doesn’t meet the standards that I think a politician at that level, a statesman, should meet. Just always wanting to get dirty, get his hands dirty in terms of insults and so on. When he was rude about Keir Starmer, I criticised him for that,” she said, adding that President Trump’s treatment of Ukraine leader Zelensky in the White House was “awful”.

The leader of the alleged Conservative Party went on to suggest that she may have even preferred to have seen Kamala Harris win the 2024 presidential election, saying: “People ask me, who did I prefer Kamela Harris, Donald Trump, and I would say I like them both equally. Make of that what you will… there’s a double meaning in that.”

Since becoming leader of the Tories in 2024, Badenoch has seen her party fall behind Nigel Farage’s Reform UK in the polls, largely because her party has failed to deliver on immigration.

Despite claiming to be a “conservative”, Badenoch personally lobbied to lift the cap on the number of work visas issued annually in 2018. She then served in the Boris Johnson government, which refused to put any cap on immigration numbers in his post-Brexit immigration changes, allowing for millions of migrants to flood into the country in one of the largest waves in British history.

Badenoch has since claimed that the government actually wanted to lower immigration, but that because there were “so many other things” going on that “ministers didn’t notice” that immigration had skyrocketed under their watch.

In his first interview following the midterm elections, Mr Farage told the BBC President Trump deserves credit for accomplishments, noting that the “American economy has been booming”, that the United States is “now an exporter of energy, not an importer”, and that he managed to close the Southern border after Biden allowed in millions of illegal migrants.

However, the Reform UK leader said that many American voters felt as though the president had “broken” the promise of not starting any new wars.

“No more foreign wars was at the heart of everything he’d said since 2015. Now look, the idea of launching strikes to stop Iran getting a nuclear weapon, I was supportive of, but we’re now eight and a half months into a prolonged war that has led to increased prices, you know, gas, diesel, Americans putting in their cars. And that’s at the heart of why he’s done badly. He’s seen by many voters to have broken that promise,” he said.

Mr Farage added that while he has not spoken to his longtime political ally since the elections, he expects a “very sharp increase in military action in Iran” in the coming days.

Pressed on whether he would advise against doing so, the Brexit leader said: “I think all the mistakes of the last 25 years that Britain and America have made often together have been because there’s been no actual exit plan. If they’ve got a clear plan, it’s fine. But remember, this isn’t like Gaddafi. This isn’t like Saddam, where you get rid of a dictatorial head and the whole regime collapses. This is a theocracy. It’s a very different battle, and I would suspect a very hard one to win.”

The leader of the so-called Conservative Party, Kemi Badenoch, said U.S. President Donald Trump deserved to lose in the mid-term elections.

news.title: Fraudulent Transfer of $26 Million Kept Secret in a New Jersey Township Until After the Election
news.text:
Residents in a small New Jersey township are outraged after they were treated to a post-election surprise: Some $26 million was stolen in a fraudulent wire transfer and was kept secret for weeks until after they decided who would run the municipality at the polls.

No one has explained why the massive theft wasn’t disclosed before the election, Fox News Digital and other outlets reported, in a debacle that now is making national headlines because of its suspicious timing.

It was only on Friday that Cranbury Township Mayor Lisa Knierim announced that the municipality had been hit by a “sophisticated financial theft,” according to an official statement released by her office.

The New Jersey Democrat said the transfer took place on September 28, tapping funds originally meant for purchasing property to “meet the township’s affordable housing obligations,” according to Fox.

The township, with a population of only 4,000 residents, is located about 20 miles northeast of Trenton.

County, state and federal law enforcement agencies, spearheaded by the township’s police department and the Middlesex County Prosecutor’s Office, have been organized into a task force to recover the funds, according to the mayor’s statement.

Investigators so far have frozen nearly $17.3 million in assets, leaving approximately $8.7 million outside the reported freeze, according to the statement, which doesn’t make clear whether that money has actually been recovered.

Knierim’s announcement came November 6, which was three days after the midterm elections and more than five weeks after the fraudulent transfer. It has not been reported by the mayor’s office or news outlets who fraudulently transferred the funds.

Several residents slammed the announcement on the township’s Facebook page, questioning why the crime was kept secret.

All five seats on the township board occupied by Democrats.

“Just another local example of one party rule and what it gets you,” wrote one critic “Will voters ever wake up and see that both parties are corrupt and must be governed by mutual distrust?”

“I’m interested in knowing why this information was kept under wraps until after Election Day,” another wrote.

Another asked, “If this occurred on September 28th why is it just now being shared?”

“What the absolute hell?” wrote another.

At stake in the midterm election was the total Democratic control the Cranbury Township Committee, its ruling body.

Democrat Thomas Szczur Jr. defeated Republican Carol Haring with 63.69% of the vote to Haring’s 36.32%, according to election results published by the New Jersey secretary of state’s office. The win preserved the Democrats occupation of all five seats on the committee.

According to the New Jersey Globe: “The victory preserved Democratic control in a township that has shifted from a swing community into a reliably Democratic municipality. the New Jersey Globe wrote. Kamala Harris carried Cranbury by 24 points in 2024, while Gov. Mikie Sherrill won it by 23 points in 2025.”

In her announcement, the Mayor Knierim said that the “immediate priorities” of officials was to pursue “every available avenue for financial recovery, and ensuring continuity of municipal operations.”

Ironically, she also promised transparency.

“We remain committed to providing accurate, timely information to the public while respecting the integrity of the ongoing investigation,” Knierim said.

news.title: Hardly Anyone Believes UFC CEO Dana White Is Actually Trump’s Pick for Press Secretary
news.text:
It’s been six years since Team Trump famously mixed up a Four Seasons hotel with a landscaping company of the same name, but the post-election gods may have presented us with an even funnier flub this year.

On Saturday (the exact anniversary of Four Seasons Gate), Trump announced UFC CEO (and domestic abuser) Dana White was his pick for White House propaganda press secretary, sparking concerns across the country. “The Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job,” Trump posted on Truth Social, floating also the names of several MMA competitors as White’s potential “assistants.” “We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left.” He added: “Dana, please take the job!” 

Thing is, even for Trump, White’s name seemed wildly out of left-field—and several social media users started theorizing whether Trump misread a short-list of candidates before mixing up UFC Dana White with Dana W. White—an assistant to the war defense secretary for public affairs, and whose background includes working with the Heritage Foundation and Fox News. 

“It is way too easy to imagine that someone recommended dana w white (who is actually a comms pro and used to work at dept of defense) to trump and trump decided to run with dana white the UFC chud,” one BlueSky user posted.

“Apparently ‘Dana W. White’ who ran public affairs for Sec Def was recommended on a short list for Trump to put as Press Secretary,” a Twitter user chimed in, adding that forming staff—and shortlists—is a job for White House chiefs of staff; not unlike the one Trump just fired on Friday. 

“Someone told Trump to pick DoD Spox and ex-House GOP flak Dana White as Press Secretary and he thought they meant Dana White the CEO of UFC,” Conor Rogers, a political strategist who previously worked on the Kamala Harris campaign, added. 

To be clear, this is all Internet hearsay—and there’s so far zero confirmation on whether Trump actually confused Dana White with Dana W. White. Jezebel has reached out to the White House for comment, and we’ll update this story if we hear anything. 

The worst of all this, however, is that we’ve no idea how seriously White’s taken his very-real job offer—and to what degree he might be considering it. He reportedly plans to meet with Trump on Monday at the White House, and earlier on Saturday, he posted to his Instagram story a seemingly AI-generated picture of himself at the lectern, writing: “on to the next chapter” (it’s not clear if he was actually joking). Speaking to CNN, however, one person familiar with the matter says White’s turned Trump’s offer down. 

Which, hopefully, is true. And while the timeline where Press Secretary Dana White’s job was over before it even started isn’t quite a “Zacharia,” it’ll do.

news.title: Ossoff And AOC Tipped As Favorites For The 2028 Democratic Presidential Nomination At Progressive Convention
news.text: Following a series of stunning Democrat victories in Republican strongholds in Tuesday's midterm elections, speculation about who the Democratic party will pick as their presidential nominee in 2028 is growing.At Crooked Con, a post-midterms progressive political convention held in Washington D.C. between Thursday and Saturday which gathered a variety of progressive and generally Democrat-aligned activists, politicians, strategists, and journalists, attendees voted in a straw poll asking them who their first choice would be for the Democratic presidential nomination.The results, declared on Saturday, showed newly re-elected Senator for Georgia Jon Ossoff leading the poll with 38.4% of votes, followed by Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez with 16.6% and former U.S. Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg with 13.9%. The remainder of the candidates, including California Governor Gavin Newsom, Illinois Governor JB Pritzker and 2024 presidential candidate and former Vice President Kamala Harris, all gained less than 5%.Although the poll is an informal one, it offers insight into which candidates enjoy the most internal support within the Democratic party and which are seen as the most capable political contenders against the GOP.Ossoff topping the poll is unsurprising; with 99% of votes counted, AP reports Ossoff having won his re-election to the Upper House by a margin of 18 percentage points.The size of the victory is notable as Georgia is a swing state that traditionally leans red, having only voted for two Democratic candidates in the last 11 presidential elections."He won by what was like 16, 17, 18 points or something. He seems like the uniformly 'compromise candidate' between the progressive and the more centrist factions of the party. And he seems very talented," statistician and election analyst Nate Silver told Crooked Con.However, Ossoff ruled out running for the top office as recently as October, stating during a Senate election debate with his Republican challenger Mike Collins that he had "zero interest in running for president."Ocasio-Cortez, known commonly as AOC, is also an unsurprising runner-up.The New York representative is a popular voice firmly on the progressive wing of the party, which was buoyed in the buildup to the midterms by primary victories for many of its prominent candidates, including Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Angie Nixon in Florida.Ocasio-Cortez's $1 million donation to El-Sayed's campaign was also widely seen as proof of her presidential intentions."When you write a check for $1 million, the assumption is she's running for president. [Michigan] is one of the first primaries, and giving a million means she has a national agenda,"one Democratic insider told the New York PostOcasio-Cortez also said as recently as September that she was, amongst other things, considering a run for the presidency in her political future.
news.summary: Newly reelected Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff and progressive titan Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez led an informal Crooked Con straw poll on potential 2028 Democratic nominees.
news.author: Raphael McMahon

news.title: How James Talarico and Abdul El-Sayed won over disillusioned Black voters
news.text:
To win his U.S. Senate race in Texas last week, Democrat James Talarico, who’s white, had to mend some fences with Black voters after he defeated Rep. Jasmine Crockett, who’s Black, in the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate. There were already hard feelings between Black voters and Democrats left over from 2024. Some prominent party members had blamed Vice President Kamala Harris’ loss to Donald Trump on “wokeness,” which Black voters rightly read as code for “Black issues.” Also, because Black women have so reliably voted for Democrats, many of them in Texas were offended at the seemingly reflexive claim by some Democrats at the start of the primary between Crockett and Talarico that he was the more electable one.

The lingering bitterness from Black voters forced him to engage in what can be described as a racial reconciliation-oriented campaign strategy.

Talarico had won the majority of white Democrats and Latinos in winning the nomination, but the lingering bitterness from Black voters forced him to engage in what can be described as a racial reconciliation-oriented campaign strategy to make up with Black voters without losing the support among of the groups he carried to win the nomination. His victory over Republican Ken Paxton to become the first Democrat to be elected to the U.S. Senate from Texas in 36 years, proves his strategy succeeded.

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed didn’t defeat a Black candidate on his way to winning his party’s nomination for U.S. Senate in Michigan, but he did have to appeal to Black voters who felt that Harris lost Michigan because Arab and Muslim voters punished Harris for President Joe Biden’s Gaza policy. El-Sayed, who himself had been slow to come around to Harris, also had to confront long-simmering tensions between Black and Arab communities in Michigan. El-Sayed also had to withstand criticism that he was antisemitic and hold on to Jewish voters and white voters who ranged from progressive to moderate.

The point here isn’t just that two Democratic candidates on opposite ends of the country had to excite Black candidates who might have been presumed to vote for their party. It’s that everybody needs to be persuaded — and that is the very point of politics. 

As obvious as that might sound, Talarico said something about Black voters before the election that one rarely hears a Democrat, or anybody else, say. He said, “We have to start treating Black voters as swing voters.”

You can argue that Donald Trump did just that in 2024, even as he ran against Harris, an HBCU graduate who was trying to become the first woman, the first Black woman and first Asian woman to serve as president. As I noted after Trump’s January 2025 inauguration, his 2024 coalition was multi-cultural and cut across class. Trump got 13% of the Black vote and 46% of the Hispanic vote, a 5-point increase with Black voters and a 18-point increase with Hispanic voters, and he was right to credit voters from those two groups for his win. But then he made Black and Hispanic voters a promise he didn’t keep: “I’ve heard your voices in the campaign and I look forward to working with you in the years to come.”

No one goes into a big tent unless they are invited in, but it’s also true that they don’t stay unless they are given a reason.

No one goes into a big tent unless they are invited in, but it’s also true that they don’t stay unless they are given a reason, and Trump’s economic policies drove up Black unemployment and his immigration policies gave Hispanic Americans a reason to fear being snatched off the streets. It shouldn’t be surprising that the newly won voters from those demographics stayed such a short while.

MS NOW’s Hayes Brown noted Thursday that Republicans, especially in Texas, based their mid-decade redistricting gerrymanders on the increased support Hispanic voters gave them in 2024. That is, they were seemingly of the belief that the way that group voted in 2024 is the way it always would, but it is the height of folly to assume the loyalty of any community to a party. Millions of 2012 Obama voters supported Trump in 2016 and, in the midterms, millions of 2024 Trump voters supported Democrats in places like Texas. 

Some Republicans clearly saw it coming. Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, R-Fla., a Trump loyalist, drew lots of attention when she ran an ad saying that President Trump’s policies had gone too far. As of Friday evening, her race against Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez was still listed as too close to call.

Republicans have also long assumed that white working-class and middle-class voters are permanently theirs, too, but the MS NOW Voter Poll revealed a softening of support since 2024.

How will the Republican Party respond? Will it ask the hard questions concerning why so many of the voters who walked into its tent in 2024 walked out two years later or will it resort to coping narratives that resist introspection? El-Sayed and Talarico, faced with the possibility of Black voters defecting or staying home, asked those questions, and they won in vastly different political landscapes.

Whether the communities in question are Black or otherwise, the days of politicians expecting their unconditional support ought to be over. Talarico made that point when he said he was treating one of the Democrats’ most reliable blocs, Black voters, as swing voters. May this be our new normal.
news.author: Erum Salam

news.title: JD Vance couldn’t save Republicans. Can he save himself before 2028?
news.text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Vice President JD Vance huddled in the East Room of the White House with President Donald Trump and other members of the administration, watching the GOP’s stunning midterm election losses roll in.

First, the House fell, then the Senate. A landslide wiped out Republican lawmakers in deep-red states and districts Trump and Vance had personally campaigned in.

Vance entered the midterms facing questions about whether he could win over Trump’s coalition and keep Secretary of State Marco Rubio from challenging him in the party’s next presidential contest. 

By the time his 2028 audition was over, he had a much bigger issue: Influential Republicans were writing off his anticipated bid altogether.

The midterms were a “clear repudiation” of the Trump administration’s tactics, Tony Perkins, a leading social conservative, said the morning after the election.

“I don't see someone within the Trump administration being the flag bearer for the conservative movement in 2028,” the Family Research Council president added. 

In the days since, leading Republicans have described the midterm wipeout in apocalyptic terms – and opened up a debate about the wisdom of the Trump administration’s second-term approach.

Some are calling for a competitive presidential primary, and pointing the finger at Vance. The vice president, in turn, sought to do damage control the morning after the election in a lengthy social media post.

The missive on his personal account blamed the war Trump started in Iran for the GOP’s midterm shellacking, drawing an apparent contrast with a president to whom he’d been unfailingly loyal publicly, even as he critiqued the conflict in private.

Long-term frustration from voters and party leaders over the war and the midterm losses could be especially consequential for Vance, as Trump’s top lieutenant and a leading booster for administration policies. It shattered the MAGA coalition the vice president hoped to inherit. 

“The scale of the Republican defeat is so great that it makes the race for the GOP presidential nomination wide open,” former House Speaker Newt Gingrich, a Trump ally whose wife is Trump’s ambassador to Switzerland, wrote on social media.

Gingrich warned that Sens. Ted Cruz and Tom Cotton, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin – even Trump’s embattled Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth – were among “a surprising number of people [who] may decide this is their chance to take advantage of the chaos.” 

Vance Spotlight: Is MAGA ready to embrace JD Vance? Midterms test VP's 2028 appeal

‘The bench strength is so good’

Vance’s navy blue, dark red and gold-painted airplane came to halt at the Toledo Express Airport. The soundtrack from “Top Gun” pulsated throughout the hangar. 

The vice president had arrived in his home state to campaign for GOP Sen. Jon Husted and gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy on the eve of the election. 

At a glance, the campaign blitz showed promise – Vance was attracting decent crowds at lunchtime rallies. He’d knock down the intermittent protester by making them the punchline of his speech.

He was raising fistfuls of cash for the Republican National Committee, where he served as finance chair, and breaking new ground for himself by acting as Trump’s fraud czar. 

But under the surface, trouble was brewing with the MAGA, evangelical and the white working-class voters he’d be counting on to make up his base of support.

After a primetime midterm convention address, 19 election rallies and nearly two years in office, even enthusiastic Vance supporters were still weighing him against the rest of the Republican lineup.

In Swanton, David Russell, a 65-year-old retiree from northwest Ohio, searched through his phone for a photo he took with Vance when the vice president was his senator. He said he’d like to see Vance seek higher office.

“Yeah, but I’ve got to be honest, the bench strength of the Republican Party is so strong. I don’t know yet ... I mean, I want him to run, I want Rubio to run,” Russell said, bringing up Vance’s chief rival unprompted. 

“We’ve got a problem, we’ve got too many A-players,” Russell said at the rally on Nov. 2.

Mary Cooperwaser of Ann Arbor, Michigan, said Vance would have her support if he were the nominee, but she’s currently torn between him and Rubio. The retired college fundraiser, who came to Ohio to see the vice president, ultimately assessed: “Whoever’s first in line, which is Vice President Vance. I think that it would be a fabulous ticket if they were both on it.”

Earlier in the day, at a rally in support of a die-hard Trump candidate in New York, Vance found a friendly crowd as he leaned into his surroundings and called the Democrat running for Congress “an asshole.” 

"Listen to your parents," Vance told children attending the morning event. "Do not talk like the vice president.”

More: Marco Rubio addresses speculation about 2028 presidential run

Sharon Stevens, 70, a retired postal worker from Pratts Hollow, New York, said she’d only seen Vance on television and came to the event because she wanted to see the VP in person. 

Vance would get her vote if he runs, Stevens said. “He believes in a lot of the stuff that Trump believes in, and I like Trump.”

'Trump would knife him’

Just how much political capital the midterm campaigning bought Vance is up for debate. Many of the candidates who were on the ballot in areas where he and Trump campaigned went down in the blue tsunami.

The GOP lost seven Senate seats and more than 40 House races in the midterm blowout that outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, a possible 2028 candidate, called an “extinction-level event.”

Ohio Republican Party chairman Alex Triantafilou, a Vance supporter, said in an interview before the election that headwinds facing Husted were part of “a classic midterm environment.” 

Husted was facing off against former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who was defeated in the 2024 election, when Democrats across the country went down with former Vice President Kamala Harris.

“We knew it'd be a dog fight. Every midterm is,” he said. “Generally speaking, I mean, it's a place where races can be competitive.”

The sitting vice president’s predicament drew comparisons to Harris from Republicans who spoke on the record or requested anonymity to speak about the 2028 election. Harris struggled with how to differentiate herself from an unpopular president, and her short-lived presidential bid later tanked.

Vance Interview: JD Vance for president in 2028? It starts with MAGA voters — and Trump

She was either unable or unwilling to separate herself from former President Joe Biden, ex-Trump national security adviser John Bolton said. 

“I’m not sure Vance even has that option,” he said, adding, “if he did try to distance himself from Trump, you know Trump would knife him.”

A close ally of the vice president argued that he’d already demonstrated that he can differentiate himself from Trump by speaking directly to disaffected voters about the economy.

Another predicted that new pathways would open up next year for the VP to draw contrasts between himself and Democrats in control of Congress.

In Ohio, where Vance, the state’s one-time senator, has a political profile of his own, he has come under scrutiny for a stance he took in the state’s gubernatorial race.

He ripped into Republicans for criticizing a controversial Ramaswamy ad that featured Democratic candidate Amy Acton’s estranged mother calling Acton a liar. Acton was removed from her mother’s home after she accused her stepfather of raping her. He was charged but fled the state. Acton’s mother remained married to him until his death.

Vance spoke out before Trump, who later encouraged Ramaswamy to keep the ad up.

“I think he’s damaged himself,” former GOP Rep. Fred Upton of Michigan said of Vance. “My guess is it’s poisoned the waters.”

Upton added, “People don’t have the stomach for that crap … it’s going to haunt him, it’s going to stick.”

Former New Jersey Republican Gov. Chris Christie called Vance’s support of the ad “a disgrace” in commentary on ABC News. 

“Vivek Ramaswamy will be forgotten. He is going to be sent to the dustbin of history,” Christie said. “But JD Vance is going to be remembered, I think, from this campaign, for more than anything else … that he stood by that ad, a man who wrote a book on Catholicism.”

Vance allies batted down the criticisms as primarily coming from failed presidential candidates. They criticized what they described as bad-faith arguments coming from people who don’t have their finger on the pulse of the party and insisted that the attack wouldn’t resonate with voters in a Republican presidential primary or a general election.

Former Ohio Gov. Ted Strickland, a Democrat, brought up Vance’s elevation of the baseless claim in 2024 that Haitian migrants in Springfield, Ohio, were eating pets.

“He has continued to operate in that way. His endorsement of this Ramaswamy ad, it's really pathetic,” Strickland said. “I think the guy’s lost his way.”

Since he became vice president, Vance’s unfavorable rating has risen sharply, increasing by roughly 10 points in the two years since his inauguration, surveys show.

Vance shrugged off a question about his approval rating on the eve of the election, saying he doesn’t put much thought into it. 

“I just try to do my job, and obviously, the American people can make the judgments they’re going to make,” he told USA TODAY after his trip to Ohio. “We just need to do good things for the American people and if we do that, I think the politics will work itself out.”

'Communion:' JD Vance on blind ambition, Catholicism and President Trump's faith

Rubio, Cruz, DeSantis are potential candidates

A couple weeks earlier, Vance said in an interview that if he ran, he expected to have Trump’s endorsement. But in comments to USA TODAY, Trump said he hadn’t even spoken to Vance about the issue. Trump said he liked Vance but also brought up cheering at his rallies for Rubio.

Rubio has brushed off 2028 talk, saying in September he has no plans to run. He didn’t rule out a presidential campaign, though, and the comments were taken as a signal by some Rubio allies that, after indicating he’d stay as long as Trump would have him and encouraging Vance to run earlier in the year, he was reassessing his options.

One Republican close to the White House said that it remains to be seen how much the outcome of the midterms would hurt Vance’s presidential prospects, noting that it was no secret that Vance had been against the war in Iran. 

The person also noted that Rubio was getting the rockstar treatment on the trail, and that he’d clearly learned a few lessons from his 2016 campaign and is displaying better political acumen.

Rubio denied last week in an interview with The New York Times that he had designs on leaving the administration. He would not talk about 2028.

Other potential 2028 contenders have been outspoken in diagnosing Republicans’ problems, with Cruz saying in a lengthy social media post that an “economic disconnect” led to the resounding defeat. 

“Tariffs have made everything too expensive, and the Iran war has dragged on too long,” Cruz said. He called it “a Watergate-level repudiation.”

DeSantis, in multiple press conferences and media appearances after the election, highlighted Florida as the only GOP stronghold to resist the blue wave. He touted his record of conservative policymaking and said GOP midterm candidates “were fighting yesterday’s battles” in focusing on culture war issues, which he championed early on. 

Vance backers argue that the vice president is still the party’s most articulate national spokesman among the potential future candidates.

“Who can keep the coalition together is the million-dollar question,” Triantafilou, the Ohio GOP chairman, said “And I think he's as strong as anyone to keep the coalition active and alive.”

Vance distances himself on Iran 

The morning after Republicans lost the midterms, Vance informed the White House he’d be issuing a statement.

He wrote on his social media account that Trump-Vance voters did show up in the midterms. He used Florida, where he said the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrats, as an example.

“But the main problem is not turnout,” he assessed. “The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.”

Vance said a pollster he respects told him the GOP’s “economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true. But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone.”

“The reason we lost is the war.” The president said so himself in interviews, he argued. 

“If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.”

Vance said voters had a right to be upset and urged them to direct their anger toward electing Republicans who share their worldview, in the post that sought to reframe the narrative about the election losses.

Russell, the retiree from northwest Ohio, said at Vance's rally that he believed the Iran war, and the vice president's involvement in the talks to end it, would not hurt Vance in the long term, because people will begin to see the benefits. 

“They took some hits with the Iran war, but I believe they had to do it, and Americans just have to stick through it,” he said.

Vance has had little to say publicly in the days since. He declined an interview request for this article. One of a handful of posts on social media was a clip of Trump being asked about his statement.

“I know how he feels about it. I think it was fine, yeah. I thought it was good. We knew that. I knew that when I went in,” Trump said of Vance’s views on Iran. 

The president’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., a close friend of Vance’s who traveled with him on the final day of the campaign, backed up the VP on social media.

At the same event with reporters, though, when Trump was asked whether he’d spoken with Vance about 2028, the president was less than supportive.

“You could have a lot of people, maybe, a lot of people running, maybe nobody's gonna run," Trump said on Nov. 4. “Maybe he won't run, I don't know who's gonna run. But I can tell you that as far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing different.”

One close Vance ally said it would be foolish for for him to make a decision based on results of the midterms, given the volatility of American politics. The person also argued that more people running would help Vance split the non-Trump administration vote.

Advisers to Vance have always maintained that the vice president had until the end of the first quarter of next year to make a decision about whether he will run. They have stressed for months that an announcement this year was not likely to come. Vance said recently that his family would be a factor, and there's a chance he wouldn't run.

Bolton, the first-term Trump national security adviser, said: “I think it’s entirely possible that when we get to late 2027, that Trump’s brand may be so toxic that people like Vance are really going to be, even if they get the nomination, they’d be very hard pressed to win.”

news.title: How the Democrats' midterm wave shows a path back to the presidency
news.text:
Although thrilled by their sweeping defeat of U.S. President Donald Trump's Republican Party in the midterms, Democrats remain cautious about jumping to conclusions of what it could mean for the next presidential election campaign. 

Still, the dramatic scale of the victory has some seeing a potential path back to the White House in 2028. 

The Democrats won the popular vote for House districts by 13 percentage points, the biggest margin for either party in 50 years. 

They ousted Republicans in Senate races in the red states of South Carolina, Texas and Kansas, which haven't sent a Democratic senator to Washington since 1998, 1988 and 1932, respectively.

Strategists are busy analyzing both what went so wrong for the Republicans and what went right for the Democrats. If there's one consistent thread in this midterm post-mortem, it's that cost of living concerns made all the difference. 

That's why leading Democrats believe the pocketbook populism that worked at the midterms in both swing states and red states is a message that could work in the next presidential election. 

Mo Elleithee, former spokesperson for the Democratic National Committee (DNC), says his party "isn't always the best at message discipline," but its candidates stayed solidly on-message in the midterm campaign.

"Candidate after candidate, the most progressive to the most moderate, from Kansas and Texas to Maine and Michigan, every Democratic candidate was talking about cost of living and corruption, and, in many cases, tying those two things together," Elleithee told PBS News Hour.

'What the future looks like'

Democrats who want to run for president will need to show voters their vision for the post-Trump era, Elleithee said. 

"For the past decade, what we have mainly been doing is playing opposition to Donald Trump," he said. "Now we can paint a picture of what the future looks like." 

For a decade, Democrats have been searching for ways to win back the many working-class voters who had abandoned them in favour of Trump. 

Their winning candidates in the midterms in red and swing states focused relentlessly on pocketbook issues in a way that could seize the terrain of economic populism back from the Trump GOP. 

"The biggest divide in this country is not left versus right. It's top versus bottom," the Texas Democrat senator-elect James Talarico said frequently from the very launch of his campaign. 

DNC chairman Ken Martin says the midterm victories were in part a repudiation of Trump, but also a consequence of Democrats talking about affordability. 

"Our candidates across the board ran for something, not against something," he told NPR. "They gave people a sense of a positive vision of what Democrats would do while we're in power."

The three priorities that Democrat leaders have said they intend to pursue immediately once the new Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3 are all aimed at bringing down costs for Americans: repealing Trump's tariffs, restoring health insurance subsidies cut by the Republicans and ending the war in Iran that triggered big jumps in fuel prices. 

Midterm results shift electoral college map

Midterm wins at the state level mean next year will see Democrat governors in power in all seven swing states that Trump won in 2024: Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, North Carolina, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. 

Democrats also now envision Ohio, which has voted solidly for Trump in three straight elections, to be a potential target in 2028 after midterm wins for both governor and Senate. 

Some are even dreaming that Texas, with its shifting demographics and its 38 electoral college votes, may no be longer a lost cause, after a Democrat sweep of statewide races. 

It remains to be seen how long the Democratic Party's midterm-fuelled unity will last once the fight for the 2028 nomination begins. 

That could start as soon as next spring, given the track record of would-be presidential candidates announcing their intentions roughly a year and a half before election day. 

Trump names Stephen Miller as new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles after midterm defeatAnalysisJD Vance blames Iran war for midterm thumping. Is he really blaming Trump?

The dominant theme in the nomination race could be the competing visions of centrist and progressive Democrats. 

Progressive icon Bernie Sanders — the independent U.S. senator from Vermont who the Democratic Party spurned in 2016 as presidential nominee in favour of establishment candidate Hillary Clinton — argues the midterm results show there's only one route to victory. 

"We can win over millions of Republicans and independents who are struggling economically if we focus on the issues that are important," Sanders told Politico Playbook this week. 

Sanders said Democrats need to have the courage to tell big-money donors, "Thank you very much for your help, but right now we are going to focus on the needs of the working families of this country, whether you like it or not."

Warnings abound for the Democrats about what lessons they should and shouldn't draw from the midterm result and how it may apply to 2028. 

David Plouffe, who served as Barack Obama's campaign manager in 2008 and advised Kamala Harris in 2024, says the Democrats can't count on voter sentiment in this year's midterms being the same in the next presidential election. 

"I would say this was a vote against Trump more than a vote for the Democratic Party. Our brand is still quite weak," Plouffe told a post-midterm forum at Harvard University's Institute of Politics. 

U.S. midterm results won't deter Trump from 'bombastic, over-the-top' style, says strategistAnalysisOhio and Texas went from red to blue in the midterms but may not stay that way in 2028

Mark Leibovich, a journalist who has extensively covered the party's Trump-era struggles, has a message similar to Plouffe's.

"Democrats should avoid the obvious trap of thinking that their victory means they've magically solved their 'brand problem,' 'trust problem,' or 'working-class-voter problem,' among various others," Leibovich wrote in the Atlantic this week.
news.author: Mike Crawley

news.title: Jennifer O'Connell: Silicon Valley’s tech bros bet everything on Trump. What will they do now?
news.text:
Spare a thought this week for Silicon Valley’s broligarchy – the tech titans who prostrated themselves so low before Donald Trump in the aftermath of the 2024 election that they’ll be seeing a chiropractor for years. 

In the coming weeks, as they desperately try to resurrect their inner Democrat and reverse the precipitous falls in their share prices, it’ll be worth reminding ourselves of a few things. Chief among these are the tech dollars that poured into Donald Trump’s inauguration fund in 2025 courtesy of Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, OpenAI chief Sam Altman, Apple boss Tim Cook and Google. 

Cook went one better – like a modern-day wise man paying homage to baby Jesus, he arrived at the Oval Office armed with gold, presenting the new president with a glass disc mounted on a solid 24-carat gold base, engraved with both men’s names. 

Bezos made an offering he deemed even better than gold, frankincense or myrrh – he sent Trump a selfie with his then-fiancee Lauren Sanchez. Over dinner with Trump, Bezos moaned about the Washington Post, the newspaper he owns, like it was his recalcitrant teenage offspring. “The people there are terrible,” Bezos said. “They don’t listen.” Amazon spent $35 million (€31 million) promoting the impressively bad “documentary” Melania. 

Perhaps the most craven of all was Zuckerberg. Trump threatened in 2020 to jail the Meta boss “for the rest of his life” if he was elected again. After the 2024 election, Zuckerberg – taking no chances – sent Trump a letter his daughter, then aged about 8, had written to the president, in which the remarkably precocious child shared how much she was “looking forward to the golden age of America”. 

But while this isn’t all that surprising from Zuckerberg – whose moral core seems forged out of Playdoh – the most puzzling broligarch conversion was that of Alex Karp, chief executive of Palantir. The one-time socialist wrote his PhD dissertation on the rhetoric of fascism, which he has said many times “terrifies” him. He supported Joe Biden and then Kamala Harris in 2024. Yet sometime over the following year he underwent a mysterious conversion that would see Palantir donate $1 million to Maga and Karp himself personally give $1 million to Trump’s inauguration committee. Palantir worked with Immigration and Customs Enforcement to target people for Trump’s mass deportation campaign, helping Trump conduct a mass surveillance campaign of Americans that a cynic might say had a distinctly fascist flavour.

Nobody was more tickled by Zuckerberg and Bezos “kissing my ass” than Trump himself, according to a book by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, Regime Change. “Think of where these guys were in 2016,” the book recounts Trump sneering to Elon Musk about Zuckerberg and Bezos. “They hated me. They were doing everything they could to knock me down. And look at them now.”

“First-class grovelling,” Musk, who would know a thing or two about it, replied.

[ Republican downfall: The inside story of Team Trump’s midterm collapseOpens in new window ]

Musk himself spent $446 million trying to get Republicans elected in the midterms (0.04 per cent of his net worth, or the equivalent of about €100 to you and me, but a lot of money to throw away nonetheless). He burned $150 million supporting Ken Paxton, who wanted Texas - Musk’s new home - to become a hub for data centres. In what would emerge as a recurring theme of the midterms, Paxton lost to James Talarico, who is promising much tighter regulation of them. Oh, and he wants to “tax trillionaires out of existence”.

What did the broligarchs get in return for these efforts? Expect the Democrats to make finding out a top priority now they’re back in control of Congress. Senator Ed Markey, a Democrat from Massachusetts, warned that “they are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing”. 

Some of it is already known. The administration took a hands-off approach on AI regulation and Trump signed executive orders to speed up permission for data centres. Democrats will almost certainly want to know more about contracts awarded to defence technology firms and manufacturing and mining companies, as well as companies with ties to Donald Trump jnr and Musk and his Doge service.

What is remarkable is not even that the tech bros didn’t appear to foresee an end to Trumpism. It’s that, for all the effort they put into harvesting our data and anticipating our every move, they overlooked the possibility that voters might choose to reject AI – a technology its own creators keep warning will guzzle power and water, potentially go rogue and hack into our private data, wipe out millions of jobs and livelihoods and may even, or so they keep saying, kill all of humanity. Perhaps that’s what happens when you run a company that treats human beings as a commodity; you tend to forget they have minds of their own.

They’re getting a loud reminder now. Many saw a sudden drop in their personal fortunes on Thursday as investors sold out of AI and chip stocks, driving the Nasdaq down more than 5.5 per cent. 

In an NBC exit poll, 56 per cent of voters said data centres and AI were “a crucial or major” factor in their vote in the midterms and more than three in four said they would oppose a data centre in their community. Talarico characterised the vote as a referendum on “the billionaires who own the social media algorithms, who own the cable news networks, who own the politicians”.

[ Democrats routed Republicans in the US midterms. But can they capitalise on it?Opens in new window ]

In the coming weeks, as the strength of voter feeling on the issue crystallises, expect to see lots of Democrats appointed to tech company boards and the role of “chief diversity officer” to once again become the fastest growing job sector on LinkedIn. The only Silicon Valley value that seems to be immutable is that ideology comes second to self-interest.
news.summary: When you run a company that treats human beings as a commodity, you tend to forget they have minds of their own

news.title: James Talarico, the new senator-elect of Texas, has a message for Trump in 'SNL' cold open
news.text: After this week's major wins by the Democratic Party in the midterm elections, it's no surprise that the cold open on "Saturday Night Live" was political in nature. But there was one surprise guest: The new senator-elect of Texas, James Talarico. The cold open began with a conversation between Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (Kenan Thompson) and Sen. Chuck Schumer (Sarah Sherman), the minority leaders of the House and Senate (and possible future majority leaders), respectively, as they celebrated their party's victory, including flipping Texas blue — for which they took credit. (Schumer: "That was all me. I found the candidates, I recruited them. And as a show of respect, they begged me not to appear at their campaign events.") Jeffries pledged that their first order of business would be to march up to President Trump and tell him, "Hey, knock it off, Buster." But Trump (James Austin Johnson), not one to be left out, interrupted to take the credit for the Democratic victories instead — thanks to the "horrible economy and terrible war." "So in the words of Moana's big fat friend, 'You're welcome,'" he said. After an appearance from J.D. Vance (Jeremy Culhane) and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth (Colin Jost), plus Trump's complaints about having to work with millennials and the return of their optimism, he began listing some of the newly elected senators who would be arriving in Washington: "Jon Ossoff, or as I call him Thinky Herman. Abdul El-Sayed, or as I call him, Mamdani for men. And of course, down in Texas, Talafreako." Talarico then stepped into frame to a roar of applause and cheers from the audience, leading to this exchange: Talarico: "Hi America, I am James Talarico, the guy who has been texting you everyday asking for $5." Trump: "In this economy, who can blame you." Talarico: "But I think Mr. President, if we can work together, we can make life better for everyday Americans. It's clear people want something new. They want something different. I'm talking of course about 'SNL's' cold opens. How many of these Trump freezes are they going to do?" Trump: "Infinity." Talarico: "Well in that case, there is only one thing to say: Live from New York, it's Saturday Night Live." It’s a notable moment for Talarico and “SNL,” which had shied away from having any cameos from politicians in the the run up to the midterms like in previous election cycles (former Vice President and Democratic nominee Kamala Harris and GOP candidate Nikki Haley made appearances during the 2024 presidential campaign). For Talarico, it marked the first time he was on a late-night network TV show since embarking on his senate campaign. Prior attempts to appear for interviews on “The Late Show With Stephen Colbert” and “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” were stymied by CBS' and ABC’s executives and lawyers, who cited threats by the FCC, led by chairman Brendan Carr, regarding the equal-time rule, which requires broadcasters to provide equal access to competing political candidates. In the past, daytime and late-night shows weren’t considered subject to the rule, but Carr has said differently. The issue also arose after Harris' "SNL" appearance. (Talarico's interviews with Colbert and Kimmel ended up on their show's YouTube accounts.) Trump has been a vocal critic of the late-night show hosts and "SNL" over the course of his tenure as president. While Talarico has called out Trump and his administration's policies in the past, his message on Saturday was much more conciliatory. Whether Trump accepts the olive branch remains to be seen.
news.summary: The senator-elect of Texas made a surprise appearance on 'Saturday Night Live,' sending a message directly to President Trump about working together for Americans.
news.author: Maira Garcia

news.title: President Trump shares claims about 'unusual patterns' in midterm elections and questions James Talarico's victory in Texas... despite saying he would accept the results
news.text:
President Donald Trump has sparked fresh controversy by sharing a series of posts questioning the results of the midterm elections, including Democrat James Talarico's stunning victory in Texas – just days after promising to accept the outcome.

The president spent part of Saturday amplifying claims about 'unusual' voting patterns, dramatic increases in Democratic support and election-night figures that some conservative commentators suggested were difficult to believe.

Trump shared several charts and messages on Truth Social that appeared to cast doubt on the scale of the Democrats' sweeping victories, which saw Republicans lose control of both chambers of Congress.

But none of the material he circulated provided evidence of election fraud or wrongdoing.

The posts mark a striking change in tone from Tuesday night, when Trump told The New York Times he was 'absolutely willing' to accept the election results and work with the incoming Democratic majorities.

One of the most provocative messages concerned Talarico's crushing victory over Trump-backed Republican Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race.

The president reposted a message from an account called The Lone Raccoon, which featured a graph showing the candidates' vote totals rising throughout election night, including several sharp jumps.

The graph highlighted sudden increases in the Democratic candidate's tally, although such jumps can occur when election officials release large batches of counted ballots.

Talarico's victory was one of the biggest shocks of Tuesday's elections, making him the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Texas since 1988.

The 37-year-old former teacher defeated Paxton by approximately 12 percentage points in a state that Trump carried comfortably just two years earlier.

Paxton has already conceded the race and congratulated his Democratic opponent.

Trump also circulated another message highlighting what its author claimed was an extraordinary surge in Democratic votes nationwide.

The post, originally published by Kevin Bass, declared: 'Republican votes stayed the same. Democrats materialized 20 million new votes.'

An accompanying bar chart compared the popular vote in House elections in 2022 and 2026.

It showed Republicans receiving 54.2 million votes in 2022 compared with a projected 55.6 million this year.

But the Democratic figures appeared dramatically different, rising from 51.3 million in 2022 to a projected 70.4 million in 2026.

Crucially, the 2026 numbers were projections based on an assumption that just 85 percent of votes had been counted, rather than final election totals.

An independent examination of the figures found that the suggestion of 20 million additional Democratic votes was misleading, with the eventual increase likely to be considerably smaller.

Trump shared a third post raising questions about the extraordinary Democratic turnout in Texas, where Republican Governor Greg Abbott was defeated by Gina Hinojosa.

The message, written by Donald Ward, noted that Abbott had actually increased his vote total compared with his successful 2022 reelection campaign.

But Hinojosa received approximately 1.7 million more votes than Democratic candidate Beto O'Rourke managed four years earlier.

'Those are Looney Tunes numbers,' Ward declared.

He also claimed Hinojosa received 400,000 more votes in Texas than Kamala Harris did during the 2024 presidential election.

'These are not normal midterms numbers,' he wrote. 'Not a single opinion poll before the elections came close to predicting this.'

Ward suggested that polling places should have experienced enormous lines to account for such high turnout.

However, comparisons between different election years do not themselves establish irregularities, and the post offered no evidence that ballots were improperly counted.

Another message circulated by Trump highlighted unusually consistent Democratic gains across multiple states and demanded closer scrutiny of ballot totals, voter records and turnout.

'A pattern this even demands answers at the ballot level,' the post declared, calling for hand counts and checks of voter registration records.

The flurry of online activity came less than four days after Trump appeared ready to acknowledge the Republicans' devastating election defeat.

'I am absolutely willing to accept those results,' he told The New York Times during a telephone interview on Tuesday night.

'We'll work with the Democrats, and we'll, you know, look forward to working with them. We'll probably work something out.'

At the time, Trump blamed Republican losses partly on his own absence from the ballot, suggesting his personal popularity could have helped struggling candidates.

He also insisted he had no regrets about supporting defeated Republicans, including Paxton and South Carolina Senator Darline Graham.

The president's latest online activity now raises questions about whether he will maintain that conciliatory position as Democrats prepare to assume control of Congress.

Their victories will give them new powers to launch investigations into his administration and potentially block key parts of his legislative agenda.
news.summary: Donald Trump shared posts questioning the midterm election results, including James Talarico's stunning Senate victory in Texas. The president highlighted claims of unusual voting patterns.
news.author: Editor,James Gordon

news.title: Amaechi: Buhari Promised Me APC Presidential Ticket in 2022
news.text:
Chuks Okocha in Abuja

The African Democratic Congress (ADC) vice-presidential candidate, Mr Rotimi Amaechi, has blamed his defeat in the 2022 All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential primary on his decision to follow the advice of the late President Muhammadu Buhari not to campaign ahead of the contest.

Amaechi said Buhari had assured him in writing that he would announce him as his preferred candidate, prompting him to refrain from lobbying delegates and negotiating political alliances ahead of the primary.

He disclosed this during an interview on Mainland 98.3FM’s The Situation Room programme in Lagos on Friday, while reflecting on how President Bola Tinubu defeated him to clinch the APC presidential ticket in 2022.

According to Amaechi, he considered Buhari’s position credible because the former president was his boss and believed his endorsement would give him an advantage over other aspirants.

He said, “The first mistake that I made at that primary was that I listened to President Buhari. He said to me, ‘don’t campaign, don’t do anything, I will announce you as my candidate.’

“He told me that. He put it in writing. When I write my book, I’ll put it out.”

The former Minister of Transportation said his decision not to negotiate political positions with governors and other influential party members also worked against his ambition, and gave Tinubu an opportunity to build alliances ahead of the primary.

Amaechi explained that he could have secured the support of governors by promising them political appointments, including the positions of vice-president and Secretary to the Government of the Federation.

 “Now, I didn’t do deals. So, I would have promised you vice-president, promised you SGF, and then would have gone for this primary, I would have possibly won. I would have had governors on my side.

“Because I didn’t do deals, Tinubu had the chance to do deals,” he said.

Amaechi, who was also a presidential aspirant in the 2022 APC primary, further accused Tinubu of exploiting religious sentiments to secure support from delegates, particularly in the North.

He, however, said he would not deploy religion as a political tool to win elections, describing his position as a reflection of his nationalist convictions.

The ADC chieftain alleged that a delegation of Southern Yoruba Muslims had approached governors in the North-West and appealed to them to support Tinubu on religious grounds.

He also cited the position of former Kaduna State Governor Nasir El-Rufai, whom he said had supported his presidential ambition before eventually backing Tinubu.

 “El-Rufai was my supporter. El-Rufai, in a viral video, said this is done for the faith,” Amaechi said.

He argued that appealing to religious identity for political support could deepen divisions in the country, adding that he would not encourage such an approach even if it offered him an electoral advantage.

“I wouldn’t want to run that kind of federation. There are 35 million Catholics in Nigeria. I wouldn’t want to go to the Catholic Church and say, ‘please announce me. Tell them that all Catholics must go out and vote Amaechi.’

“It will cause confusion. It will cause problems in the country. That makes me a nationalist,” he said.

Amaechi questioned the perception of Tinubu as an exceptionally strategic politician, asking why he had not become president earlier if his political success was based on an extraordinary ability to manoeuvre.

Tinubu defeated Amaechi and other aspirants at the APC presidential primary held at Eagle Square, Abuja, in June 2022, polling 1,271 votes against Amaechi’s 316.

Kemi Badenoch Tackles Trump, Says US President Deserves US Midterm Defeat

 Sunday Ehigiator

British Conservative Party leader, Kemi Badenoch, has said the United States President Donald Trump deserved his defeat in the country’s midterm elections, criticising his handling of the Iran war, trade policies and treatment of allies.

 The Independent reported yesterday that Badenoch described Trump’s electoral setback as “entirely self-inflicted” and condemned what she called his “dirty” style of politics.

The Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections, flipping at least seven Senate seats and more than two dozen House districts in a major setback for Trump’s Republican Party.

Asked whether Trump deserved the defeat, Badenoch, in an interview with The Independent’s Editor-in-Chief, Geordie Greig, replied, “Yeah. He has not been acting in the way that I would consider conservative.”

She criticised Trump’s tariffs, threats towards Canada and Greenland, and disputes with US allies, saying his actions contradicted conservative principles of free markets and better trade.

 “Where is the push for free markets and better trade… rather than protectionism, America first, the squabbling with allies? That’s not what conservatives do,” she said.

Badenoch also criticised Trump’s personal attacks on journalists and political figures, saying his conduct fell below the standards expected of a statesman.

“Trump is very charming in person, but you see the way that he talks about journalists, about individuals. It doesn’t meet the standards a statesman should meet – always wanting to get dirty in terms of insults and so on,” she said.

She said she was particularly unhappy with Trump’s remarks about British Prime Minister Keir Starmer and described his treatment of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at the White House as “awful”.

On the Iran war, Badenoch said she understood Trump’s initial decision to launch the military action, which she supported because of concerns about Iran acquiring nuclear weapons, but questioned the absence of a clear strategy.

“We don’t want them getting nuclear weapons. But where’s the plan?” she asked.

She also said she would have been content if Trump had lost the 2024 presidential election to his Democratic opponent, Kamala Harris.

Asked which of the two candidates she preferred, Badenoch said, “I would say I like them both equally. Make of that what you will.”

The Conservative leader also argued that Trump had squandered the broad coalition of voters that helped him win the presidency, including Latino voters and more Black voters than any previous Republican candidate.

“What’s the first thing he does? Tariffs, and then talking about Greenland and Canada. A lot of people were wondering, ‘What are you doing?’” she said.

Badenoch’s comments came amid wider criticism of Trump’s handling of the economy and foreign policy following the Republicans’ losses in the midterms.

Badenoch is the leader of the UK Conservative Party and Leader of the Opposition. She became Conservative leader in November 2024 after defeating Robert Jenrick in the party’s leadership contest. She previously served as the UK’s Business and Trade Secretary and Minister for Women and Equalities under former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak.

Badenoch, whose birth name is Olukemi Olufunto Adegoke, was born in Wimbledon, London, in 1980 to Nigerian parents.

news.title: In 2028 race, Democrats have new stars and Republicans have succession squabbles
news.text:
WARNER ROBINS, Georgia – Candy Bautista was smiling as she helped herself to some fluffy pancakes at a brunch buffet. A 23-year-old economics graduate struggling to find a job, she voted for the first time the day before, on Nov 3, not really expecting an electoral earthquake.

“But I went to bed in a red state and woke up in a blue one,” said Bautista, an independent voter.

The sentence captured Georgia’s dramatic swing in the 2026 midterm elections; it elected a Democrat as governor for the first time in over 20 years. 

An even more stunning upset was in neighbouring South Carolina, which chose a Democrat senator for the first time in nearly 30 years. 

Jordy Stevens, a nurse in Lexington, South Carolina, had something to do with it. His vote had always gone to the Republicans by default. “It is just how I was raised in a Republican family,” he said. 

“But this year, look what I did.” 

The high cost of petrol was the chief reason the 30-year-old went against his party. “They forgot about us,” he said. “Now I know what that vote is worth, and our government knows it too.”

Voters like Bautista and Stevens have scrambled President Donald Trump’s political coalition and set the pulses racing for the 2028 presidential election. 

For a decade, Trump so dominated the political landscape that others defined themselves through their opposition to him. Now, with his party chastened and his presidency approaching its term limit, other figures are becoming visible.

There are no major declared contenders yet, but Americans could find themselves spoilt for choice in 2028. 

The Democrats, riding on newfound confidence after the diminishment of 2024, have the more expansive field. The Republicans have the more formidable task: How much of the Trump baggage should they carry into 2028 and what can be safely disposed of without offending his base.

A Fox News/NORC voter study described their predicament. Nearly four in 10 Republicans from Trump’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement want his successor to adopt both his policies and his leadership style, while half want only his policies. 

Even among non-MAGA Republicans, 45% want his policies continued.

Among the independent voters, though, six in 10 want a break from both Trump’s policies and his style.

That invokes the eternal nomination problem – first rally the party faithful, then hope to succeed with voters who sneer at the faithful. 

A successful post-Trump Republican candidate can have either Trump’s coalition or the independents, the largest bloc of American voters.

Vice-President J.D. Vance, 42, has begun this negotiation. “The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote on X after the midterms. It is a useful formulation for a vice-president seeking to establish that the administration’s failure in the unpopular Iran war was not entirely his own.

But Vance has publicly defended the Iran war, whatever his reservations in behind-the-scenes White House debate. He cannot simply step aside.

Ohio adds another embarrassment. In his home state, Democrat Amy Acton defeated Vivek Ramaswamy for governor; Sherrod Brown won the Senate seat held by Vance’s appointed successor Jon Husted. 

That complicates Vance’s claim to understand the industrial Midwest, despite his hillbilly roots, and speak for the “left-behind” men and women.

Still, he remains formidable, with high visibility and access to donors. 

Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio has been quieter since the midterm election, with his aides moving quickly to quash rumours that he is leaving the administration. He has previously said he would not challenge Vance. 

Polls do not show it yet, but the popularity of the former Cuban American senator from Florida is second to none with the more traditional Republicans. And the man who inspired countless social media memes – an astronaut, the Easter Bunny and a cardinal – has ardent admirers within the MAGA alumni as well as independents. 

The 55-year-old has both youth and name recognition. I have never heard anyone ask “Rubio, who?” the way I had seen people shrug when Trump roped in Vance as his running mate in the presidential campaign of 2024. But Rubio, in charge of foreign affairs and national security, cannot dodge the Iran war taint either.

Safest from any association with the war is Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, 48. He has taken credit for Republican victories in Florida: Byron Donalds as governor and Ashley Moody for senator prevailed in tight races. 

The man behind Florida’s bitter culture wars has described party performance in the midterms as a near “extinction-level event” and a rebuke of Trump. 

Which Floridian can excite the party remains an open question; current surveys show a DeSantis surge, but Rubio maintains the lead.

The field could widen if Vance stays vulnerable. Texas Senator Ted Cruz, 55, has left the door open for another presidential run, and former UN ambassador Nikki Haley remains among the names discussed. Tucker Carlson, the former Fox News host, while denying presidential plans, could help shape the argument over foreign intervention, whether as a commentator, organiser or political insurgent. 

A 2024-type crowded race – when at least 10 high-profile candidates ran in the primaries – is plausible. So is a familiar outcome where a divided opposition allows the candidate with the most committed minority to prevail.

But the Republicans can nurture hope. A midterm loss is like being sentenced to hard labour; it is not a death sentence. After a Democratic wipeout in the 2010 midterms, Barack Obama was re-elected convincingly two years later.

Democrats: A wealth of new political talent

The Democrats have emerged from the midterms with a version of “100 ways to win an election”. Unlike the Republicans, they do not have to wrestle with the Trump deadweight, but they do have an ideological maze of their own. 

Before the election, the New York Times/Siena survey found that nearly half want the party to move towards the centre, while around a quarter want to swing left. 

Independents also give the Democrats a hard time. Nearly three in four want Democrats to move towards the centre. It is a sign that progressive politics does not really own the day.

Almost all polls ranking Democratic Party nominees currently show Georgia’s re-elected Senator Jon Ossoff, 39, at or near the top. The breakout star of the midterm election has emerged with a convincing argument for electability: An 18-point win in a presidential battleground Trump carried in 2024. 

His direct attacks on Trump’s corruption and fitness for office became the talk of the nation.

I saw him in a roomful of Democratic volunteers, rolling up their sleeves to go door-knocking on an overcast day. He spoke like Obama, but looked like a less polished but more earnest version of the Chicago senator in 2008. 

Some critics fault him for striving hard to create a perfect image, in the way that an expert film-maker would. And given his antecedents as an investigative documentary maker for eight years, perhaps the critics are not far wrong.

In a party that has not had a national leadership since the Biden presidency, he has stirred up undeniable excitement.

But is he the runaway hot favourite?

He has said he has “zero interest” in running. But political circumstances can change, and he is certainly not short on ambition.

One survey shows him on a par with five-term New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, 37. The wait is on for AOC, as she is known, to announce her run. 

The progressive politician already has national recognition, with tens of millions of social media followers, and a formidable fund-raising operation. However, beyond the liberal blue states such as New York and California, Ocasio-Cortez’s popularity remains to be tested.

A version of that question – the potential for cross-sectional appeal – also looms over Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim to be elected senator. Soon after his victory in a major battleground, he registered a political action committee, seen as a precursor to a presidential run.

Inevitably, the newly blue Texas also has its own claimant. James Talarico, 37, has created a dazzling national opportunity for himself by winning a red fort once considered impregnable by Democrats. Any argument for expanding the map in 2028 has to begin with him. After all, Texas offers the prize of the second-largest number of electoral votes, after California, in a presidential contest.

Add in his squeaky clean appeal and boyish charm, and the package is too good to miss. A short Senate apprenticeship need not prevent his advancement; Obama was a junior senator when he bid for the White House. 

Still, other surveys have favoured former vice-president Kamala Harris, 62, who retains nationwide recognition and the relationships with donors and voting blocs from her 2024 run. 

California’s outgoing Governor Gavin Newsom, 59, also has viability; he has tried to cultivate a profile through mocking confrontations with Trump, and fund raising. He has also said he would not run if Harris does.

But Harris must explain why a second presidential attempt would succeed after 2024. And Newsom must defend California’s expensive housing-and-living environment and homelessness record.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, 53, is thought to have an edge because building a Democratic presidential coalition is difficult without winning states like his. His interest is clear: He released his memoirs in January and registered a federal political committee.

His challenge, as a Jewish man, includes navigating Democratic divisions over Israel, although he opposes the Iran war.

Other governors in contention include Andy Beshear, 48, the two-time governor of Kentucky, a red state, and Illinois Governor JB Pritzker, 61, who packs an anti-Trump identity and the wealth to sustain a long campaign. 

Also popular is Pete Buttigieg, 44, former president Joe Biden’s transportation secretary and Indiana mayor, with national experience and a fund-raising network.

Former envoy to Japan and Obama aide Rahm Emanuel, 66, is considering a candidacy built around moderate renewal in opposition to candidates like Ocasio-Cortez.

As the jostling continues in the two-year marathon from now to November 2028, the Republicans must decide who can inherit Trump’s voters, while the Democrats must find someone who can unite their factious party.

Millions of voters, like Bautista and Stevens, will be watching with a renewed sense of their own power after the momentous midterms.
