news.title: Donald Trump is not impressed to be called 'a loser' by British reporter after US President suffered mid-term hammering
news.text:
Donald Trump was asked what it feels like 'to be a loser' after his party was hammered in the mid-terms this week.

The US President didn't seem impressed by the question, asked by a British reporter on Friday.

Trump simply walked off and did not respond, after previously speaking to reporters as he departed the White House for Florida.

It came after a political hammering as voters in the US took to the polls on Wednesday to vote on seats in the Senate and House. 

His party lost seats across the board, with shock wins for the Democrats in previously safe Republican states including Texas.

The Democrats now hold a majority in both chambers, with Republicans beginning a blame game and Trump ditching Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.

Voters roundly rejected the President's policies, with the war in Iran, tariffs and rising cost of living all contributing, pundits said.

Addressing reporters as he left the White House yesterday, Trump was asked about the results.

'How does it feel being a loser, Mr President?' a British journalist shouted out.

The President did not acknowledge the question and walked off, holding a large umbrella. 

And in Britain, political figures previously full of praise for Trump are already turning their backs.

Leader of the Conservatives Kemi Badenoch has described the results as 'entirely self-inflicted', telling Independent editor-in-chief Geordie Greig on The Talk Show: 'Voters want results'.

She pointed to foreign policy and the President's tariffs as key aspects of voters' dissatisfaction, as well as threats to allies including Canada and Greenland. 

She also described Trump's treatment of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in the White House as 'awful', and said she did not like how he was 'rude about [Sir] Keir Starmer'.

The Conservative leader added that she would have been content if Democratic nominee Kamala Harris won in 2024, quipping: 'I like them both equally. Make of that what you will.'

When asked if he deserved to be thrashed in the vote, she said: 'Well, yeah. He has not been acting in the way that I would consider conservative.

'Where is the push for free markets and better trade and more enforcement of trade rules, rather than protectionism, America first, the squabbling with allies? That's not what conservatives do.'

She added: 'We need to separate President Trump from the United States. The special relationship is with the country.

'When he was rude about Keir Starmer… I didn't like that at all,' she added. 'What they did to President Zelensky in the White House was awful.'

In the aftermath of the results, Vice-President JD Vance also blamed the war in Iran in a marked shift away from his previous loyalty. 

He shared a lengthy X post regarding conflict, listing all the other reasons the party lost and appealing to Republican voters to give the party another chance in the future of the MAGA movement.

'The reason we lost is the war. The President himself said so last night,' he said.

'If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,' he said.

'Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.'

And as the fallout continues, Trump announced last night that long-running Chief of Staff Susie Wiles was out, and will be replaced by Stephen Miller, the current deputy. 

Pressed on the shake-up Friday afternoon, Trump told reporters: 'I wanted to make a change. I think Susie's done a very good job, great job, but... we gotta make moves. Sometimes in life, you have to make moves.'

His account cuts against that of a senior White House official, who told the Daily Mail that Ms Wiles 'gave her resignation last night'.

While Trump says publicly that he needed to make a change, the official says that the departure was Ms Wiles' decision.

Reports suggest that Trump dramatically turned on Ms Wiles in the Oval Office, and she walked out with him still shouting at her. 

Trump had turned on his chief of staff in a meeting with other aides and berated her over the brutal outcome of the elections, four sources familiar with the argument told the Daily Mail.

She is said to have asked to stay until February, which Trump refused, before tendering her resignation. 

A White House official denied that Trump raised his voice at Ms Wiles: 'He would never yell at Susie.' 

It remains to be seen whether Ms Wiles will be the only head to roll.
news.summary: Trump simply walked off and did not respond, after previously speaking to reporters as he departed the White House for Florida.
news.author: Editor,Elizabeth Haigh

news.title: This 1 Emotion Turns People More Conservative When Threatened – And No, It’s Not Fear
news.text:
Political campaigns often run on messages of fear: In the 2024 presidential election, President Donald Trump said the country would be “finished” if Vice President Kamala Harris were elected. Harris, meanwhile, claimed a second-term Trump would walk into the Oval Office with an “enemies list” and seek revenge and “unchecked power.”

Fear-mongering messaging is effective, especially when it comes from the political right, since people tend to lean more conservative in times of external or foreign threats. For instance, after the 9/11 terrorist attacks, national polls showed that support for Republican President George W. Bush rose by 39 points to a record-breaking 90% approval rating. Temporarily, more Americans supported conservative-leaning security policies post 9/11, including the Patriot Act, which significantly expanded the surveillance and law enforcement powers of federal agencies.

Conventional wisdom assumes that it’s fear that drives shifts to the right when people feel threatened, but a study suggests it’s a different emotion in the driver’s seat: Anger. 

“Some prominent theories in social and political psychology have proposed that fear drives these effects, but surprisingly few studies have actually tested this idea,” said Alan Lambert, the co-author of the study and an associate professor of psychological and brain sciences at Washington University. 

“We did, and found that anger, far more than fear, was responsible for these threat-driven ‘shift to the right’ effects,” Lambert said. 

Specifically after terrorist attacks, people want retribution and to punish the people who did it, said Lambert, who co-authored the research with Seattle University’s Fade Eadeh.

To find that out, Lambert and Eadeh conducted three experiments with over 2,000 participants.

In the first experiment, the researchers presented participants with descriptions of realistic, but fictional, politicians espousing either conventionally conservative “hawkish” or liberal “dovish” positions. 

“Among those participants previously primed with reminders of a previous terrorist attack on the U.S., we found greater support and liking for the hawk,” Lambert told HuffPost. “This effect occurred regardless of whether the politician was identified as a Republican or a Democrat.” 

Notably, the duo found relatively little impact of fear, and this was true not only in this initial study but also in two additional experiments, which involved over 2,000 participants. 

Still, these opinion shifts were specific to the threat at hand. For instance, anger about terrorism increased support for aggressive military action against Islamist groups, but didn’t affect views on unrelated topics like abortion, corporate power or anti-Mexican attitudes tied to the border. People stayed on topic with their anger. 

Eadeh’s previous research found that anger can also drive people toward liberal views when the threat involves areas where liberals are seen as more competent, like health care or the environment. In those cases, anger shifted opinions in a liberal direction on the issues directly tied to the threat.

Although the study didn’t address it, Lambert gave some thought to how anger drove voters into Trump’s arms not once, but twice.

“Anger was a significant driver of their support for Trump, and that was true both times he was elected,” Lambert said. “But importantly, that anger was not due to terrorist attacks. Rather, it was almost certainly due, at least in part, to the anger that conservative voters felt towards Democrats.”

It’s a fascinating time to study political polarization and Lambert is keeping busy. In future studies, he said he wants to explore whether some threats might make people more set in their ways and beliefs, making liberals more liberal and conservatives more conservative.
news.author: Brittany Wong

news.title: Kemi Badenoch aims brutal dig at Donald Trump following US mid-term election thrashing
news.text: Tory leader Kemi Badenoch has said Donald Trump deserved to be thrashed in the US mid-term elections as she criticised him over the Iran war, tariffs, and threatening Canada and Greenland. The Conservative leader said the election results were “entirely self-inflicted” in an interview with Independent editor in chief Geordie Greig for The Talk Show, adding: “Voters want results.” She went on to say that the US president “doesn’t meet the standards a politician at that level, a statesman, should meet” in the way he talks about people and “always wanting to get dirty in terms of insults”. Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter Mrs Badenoch also branded Mr Trump’s treatment of Volodymyr Zelensky in the White House “awful”. She even said she would have been content if Democratic nominee Kamala Harris had won in 2024, saying: “I like them both equally. Make of that what you will.” The Tory leader said of Mr Trump: “He came in with this extraordinary coalition, Latinos, he had more black voters than any other Republican, and what’s the first thing that he does? “Tariffs and then talking about Greenland and Canada and I think a lot of people were wondering, ‘what are you doing? Tariffs are bad for the cost of living, they’re not good, then you have a war in Iran, which, I understand the justification, Iran is an enemy of this country, we don’t want them getting nuclear weapons, but where’s the plan?” Asked if he deserved to be thrashed, she said: “Well, yeah. He has not been acting in the way that I would consider conservative. Where is the push for free markets and better trade and more enforcement of trade rules, rather than protectionism, America first, the squabbling with allies? That’s not what conservatives do.” She added: “We need to separate President Trump from the United States. The special relationship is with the country. President Trump is very charming in person, but you see the way that he talks about journalists, about individuals, it doesn’t meet the standards that I think a politician at that level, a statesman should meet – always wanting to get dirty in terms of insults and so on. “When he was rude about Keir Starmer… I didn’t like that at all. What they did to President Zelensky in the White House was awful.” Mrs Badenoch also criticised former UK prime ministers in the previous Tory governments. While refusing to “name and blame” the Conservative Party ’s former leaders, she said they were guilty of “gimmicks, mistakes and short-termism”, adding: “Everyone makes mistakes. Obviously, the leaders were responsible for most of them. Immigration was too high.” Asked whether she meant the so-called “Boriswave” of immigration, she said: “People know who the prime minister was then.” On Liz Truss’ mini-budget, she said: “You can’t just announce £150 billion bailing out people’s energy bills and £45 billion of tax cuts with no spending cuts at all. Those are the wrong way of doing things.” On Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, she insisted that his explanation of the £5 million crypto donation “doesn’t add up”. She said: “One of the things going wrong for him was that he pretended to be this everyman. “A lot of his supporters… don’t understand how he’s getting £5 million and they’re not able to pay their energy bills. His story doesn’t add up.” The Tory leader was also adamant she would never serve in a government with Mr Farage as prime minister, saying: “No, because he would not be good for this country. I simply wouldn’t.” Meanwhile, she dismissed some of Reform’s ideas, such as a recent proposal to nationalise Poundland as “bonkers”, but claimed Mr Farage did her a favour with the defection of Robert Jenrick, which she said was like defusing an “unexploded bomb”. Leaks from the shadow cabinet stopped overnight, she said, joking: “The only thing I haven’t done is written a thank you card to Nigel Farage for taking these problems away. I’ll write it in his Christmas card.” On Prime Minister Andy Burnham , she said he is more “fun” than Sir Keir Starmer, but that this “makes him more dangerous because he wants to please everybody”. Branding Mr Burnham a “foot in mouth” politician, she said: “He says things first and then thinks about it later.” Declining to to apologise for calling Bridget Phillipson “spiteful” over VAT on private school fees, she said: “Spiteful. What’s wrong with that?” She added: “She hurt many, many children. They had to leave their schools, which closed down. It was class war. So yes, I will call it like it is. “We’ve spent a lot of time dressing things up in fancy words where most of the public don’t understand what we’re talking about.” Mrs Badenoch also said she has “never” experienced racism in Britain. She told The Talk Show: “Never. That is the honest truth. It’s one of the reasons I say that this is an amazing country. This is not a racist country. “Of course there are racists. There have been people who have said and done things which I would’ve thought, yes, this is prejudice. “But my definition of racism is people who would deliberately disadvantage you because of your race, not somebody making an off-colour joke.” She added: “Did anyone ever use the N-word to me? No. Never. Only black people – and not in a hostile way. “Have I had people who I think may have disliked me because of the colour of my skin? Probably, but I can’t prove it because they didn’t show it.”
news.summary: 'Entirely self-inflicted'
news.author: Abbie Llewelyn

news.title: As the Trump Era Ends, We’re Still Living in Leonard Cohen’s Future
news.text: Like father, like son. Tonight, at Meridian Hall in Toronto, Adam Cohen will take to the stage to sing Leonard Cohen’s songs, having modestly said, “I happen to have inherited his body type and his voice.” The show, Everybody Knows, recalls a song his father co-wrote in 1988 and it marks exactly ten years since his death. The Canadian troubadour passed in his sleep at his home in Los Angeles on November 7, 2016, after a fall during the night. He was 82. The next day, Americans elected Donald Trump. The news of Cohen’s death was not made public until after the vote, so many of his fans (perhaps “fellow travelers” is a better phrase, however indelicate) took in the two events in the same week. Cohen never spoke publicly about Trump. He didn’t have the chance, but perhaps he never would have taken it anyway. His final album, You Want It Darker, was released just three weeks before his death. That autumn he told The New Yorker, “I am ready to die. I hope it’s not too uncomfortable.” A few days later, at the Canadian consulate in Los Angeles, he took it back: “I’ve always been into self-dramatization. I intend to live forever.” Even when discussing his own mortality, that was typical of the man. He had spent decades declining to be pinned down—personally, sensually, religiously—and once said he had tried to “define a political position that no one can decipher.” What he left more indelibly were songs, some of them written 30 years before his death, about walls coming down, plagues arriving, and the base human hunger for extremes. Over the decade that began the morning after he died, the Trump era kept handing those songs back to his listeners and the America that emerged. Cohen had a phrase not dissimilar to Trump’s inauguration lament about the “American nightmare” for the condition he thought the world was in. “The catastrophe has already happened,” he said, and the only question left was how to cope. His answer was idiosyncrasy. America’s answer, increasingly, appears to be certainty, not least among the cultural and political voices who’ve come to crowd out everyone else. Songs do not remain fixed in the time in which they are written but wait for the world, and the people listening, to change around them. Sometimes they become more comforting, sometimes more troubling. Few of Cohen's songs have had to wait so long, ironically, as “The Future.” The Future “The Future,” the swirling, smouldering title song of Cohen’s 1992 album, was written amid the reckoning of the L.A. riots. For Cohen, those events foreshadowed a greater reckoning. The song seems to suggest a world in which morality had become exclusively relativistic, even to the extent of murder, and its narrator longs for the trifecta of the Berlin Wall, Stalin and St. Paul, because “things are going to slide, slide in all directions” as the “blizzard of the world” overwhelms everything, including the soul itself. In 1992, there was no social media, no artificial intelligence, no content algorithms, not even the internet, or at last not as we would recognize today. If the blizzard of the world was overwhelming back then, it was a breeze compared to what followed. But more pertinent still was the collapse of moral order, as Cohen saw it. And Trump, whatever his policy achievements or failures, saw that instinctively, from the other side. He saw it among his supporters too. Hence, months before Cohen’s death, he could say: “I could stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot somebody, and I wouldn't lose any voters, OK?” Morality was applied differently depending on to whom it was applied, even to the extent of murder. But even on such matters, Cohen defied glib categorization. After his death, it was revealed he was a card-carrying member of the National Rifle Association, alongside his involvement with Buddhism. There was, though, a particular moment behind Cohen's foreboding. The old certainties were already beginning to crumble. And, as “The Future” suggests, nowhere was that more visible than in the sudden disappearance of the most imposing physical symbol of the world he had grown up in. The Walls Cohen began writing “Democracy” in late 1989, as the Berlin Wall came down and the West celebrated. He later described himself as “that gloomy fellow who always turns up at a party to ruin the orgy.” He told the songwriter and journalist Paul Zollo that he expected “a lot of suffering will be the consequence of this wall coming down.” Not because he supported the Soviet Union, but because an age of superpower competition defined by mutually assured destruction gave a sense, illusory as it was, of moral stability. He wrote roughly 60 verses before he finished. He asked himself where democracy was really arriving and settled on the United States, the place where races, classes, genders and sexual orientations meet. He called it “the real laboratory of democracy.” Twenty-four years later, Trump ran for president on a promise to build a wall of his own, along the southern border, partly due to what he saw as a laboratory experiment out of control. Four years after that, on January 6, 2021, a crowd of his supporters rampaged through the walls of the Capitol to stop Congress from certifying his democratic defeat. Cohen did not live to see Russian forces cross other walls into Ukraine. In 2022, Wayne Robins, who interviewed him when The Future came out, went back to the record and wrote that it had taken on new weight as war spread across Eastern Europe and American democratic norms came under strain. But Cohen's anxiety wasn’t confined to the fate of political institutions or to borders being redrawn. He was really interested in what happened inside people when the walls fell away: the seductions of certainty and the peculiar glamour that extremism can acquire. The Appetite “First We Take Manhattan,” the opening track of 1988’s I’m Your Man, is sung by a man promising to seize control of two particularly pungent cultural petri dishes, Manhattan and Berlin. Backstage that year, Cohen was blunt: “It is a terrorist song.” To Zollo he explained more. He said the most compelling energy of the age came from the extremes, and that he had to resist being drawn toward them in his own mind. The song, he said, was addressed to everyone who shares that fascination, and it was better to satisfy an appetite for extremism in a song than to blow up a bus full of schoolchildren. An extremist view identified in the song was to be guided by “the beauty of our weapons.” In April 2017, five months after Cohen died, Trump ordered 59 Tomahawk missiles fired at a Syrian airbase. On MSNBC, as the launch footage played, Brian Williams said “I am tempted to quote the great Leonard Cohen” before reciting the song’s line. That June, Trump told the Emir of Qatar they would discuss buying “lots of beautiful military equipment.” In January 2020, threatening Iran, he promised to send some of America’s “brand new beautiful” equipment its way. That likely wasn’t the kind of beauty Cohen had in mind. There was undoubtedly something more there: a recollection of W. B. Yeats’ “terrible beauty,” not merely admiration or wonderment. Violence was one expression of the disorder Cohen anticipated. But he was also interested in the quieter ways a society could come apart: the loss of trust, the spread of fear, and the sense that something was wrong even when nobody could quite say what it was. The Plague “Everybody Knows” describes a captain who lied and a plague moving fast. Cohen said “The plague in the most physical sense is AIDS.” He meant something wider too, describing “a plague of alienation and separation and lassitude and panic” beneath it. The same song opens with loaded dice and a fight everybody knows was fixed. It’s difficult not to see the loaded dice as being a broadside against inequality. That’s something Trump also criticized, even as he lauded stock market gains whose benefits are concentrated among millionaires and billionaires. Yet Trump spent the months after the 2020 election insisting the dice had been loaded against him. Cohen had been dead for more than three years when Covid-19 arrived. By March 2020, writers were noting that the song might as well have been written about it. Trump reached for the same word. In an April 2020 interview with Bob Woodward, recorded while he was pressing for the country to reopen, he said “It is the plague.” At rallies that year he told supporters there were many names for the virus: “I call it the plague from China. The plague.” Cohen never seemed interested in telling his audience what to think and was suspicious of the idea that an artist should provide such answers. The generations that followed him have been rather less reticent. As American politics became increasingly difficult to separate from popular culture, musicians found themselves not merely commenting on the political moment but choosing sides in it. The Endorsers Cohen predicted the coming rejection of doubt, which mutated into the rejection of truth as “fake news.” The artists who came after him have been less guarded. In the 2024 presidential race, Taylor Swift posted her hubristic endorsement of Kamala Harris minutes after the September debate, writing that Harris “fights for the rights and causes I believe need a warrior.” Bruce Springsteen backed Harris and said “Donald Trump is running to be an American tyrant.” Beyoncé let Harris use “Freedom” in her first campaign ad. Trump drew his musicians largely from country and rap. Kid Rock performed before Trump’s acceptance speech at the 2024 Republican convention, and Lee Greenwood introduced him on two nights. Kid Rock put his reasons simply: “I want that guy on my team.” Kid Rock, Jason Aldean, Greenwood and Billy Ray Cyrus all appeared at inauguration events in January 2025, as did the tenor Christopher Macchio, who sang the national anthem. Macchio had sung Cohen’s song “Hallelujah” at the 2020 Republican convention. Cohen's music has always belonged, liked any music, partly to the people who listen to it. But that doesn't mean every use of it is an act of understanding. The Borrowed Hymn “Hallelujah” was the song in which the orbits of Trump and Cohen did collide. The Republican National Convention played it twice in 2020 even after Cohen’s estate had refused permission. The estate’s lawyer, Michelle Rice, replied that if the party had asked for “You Want It Darker” instead, “we might have considered approval of that song.” In October 2024 the estate had Sony send the Trump campaign a cease-and-desist letter, and Rufus Wainwright said he was mortified that his own cover had been played at a campaign event. In June this year, ahead of a rally in Washington marking the country’s 250th birthday, Cohen’s estate issued a statement: “This use is not authorized, and the Estate does not support or approve” it. The song was performed anyway, as a beautiful B-2 bomber flew overhead. Hallelujah for the war with Iran was not what Cohen had in mind, though we can’t be sure. After all, he did once perform for Israeli soldiers in the Yom Kippur War of 1973, and returned a changed and reinvigorated man. Yet it would be a mistake to leave Cohen in the company of those who foresaw catastrophe and had nothing to offer beyond the warning. Darkness was never everything. The Crack Cohen had an answer for despair too, and it came on the same album as “The Future.” Of “Anthem,” he said, “The future is no excuse for an abdication of your own personal responsibilities.” In the week he died, its lines about the crack that lets the light in spread across the internet. In 2014, when a reporter suggested his new songs carried a hidden hope amid the darkness, he answered, “I’m a closet optimist.” There’s much to be said for optimism. There’s also much to be said for doubt. The confusion of America in the Trump era was that so many people thought the latter must negate the former. Ten years after his death, we are still trying to make sense of the future Cohen described. Perhaps that is why his songs endure: not because they tell us what is going to happen, but because they remind us that we might not know. In an age of extremes, everybody thinks they know. They can't all be right, all the time.
news.summary: Cohen died the day before Donald Trump was first elected. The songs he left have been keeping time ever since.

news.title: The 2028 GOP Presidential Primary Is Here, and It Kicked Off With an … Essay Contest?
news.text:
Welcome to this week’s edition of the Surge, a politics newsletter that totally predicted Democrats would get 260 House seats and 56 Senate seats in our heads weeks ago but, you know, didn’t feel like telling anyone.

Well that was sump’m else, huh? Crazy to think that Democrats were toast two years ago and that, starting in January, every American will be required to pledge daily allegiance to a nonbinary god. But anyway, the 2026 midterms are old news—what’s going on with the 2028 Republican presidential field? And could Democrats have picked up more than a measly nine Senate seats? Will anyone not vote to impeach Pete Hegseth?

Let’s first look ahead to what Democrats are planning to do with these majorities beyond passing national Sharia law.

What matters now: So what are these Democrats going to do?

If there’s any downside to flipping (likely) nine Senate seats and winning the largest House majority this century, it’s convincing the voters who brought you there that they’ve already seen the greatest accomplishments of the next two years.

The very act of winning ends Republicans’ partisan legislative agenda. It ends Donald Trump’s ability to gift 37-year-old brainmelt cases lifetime appointments to the federal bench. Trump will not be able to get another Supreme Court nominee confirmed come January. He will not be allowed to do as he pleases with the understanding that congressional committees will willingly ignore it. The most important elements of the incoming Democratic agenda, in other words, have already been completed.

In terms of how Democrats will spend their next two years in Congress, though, there’s not much to overthink.

They were elected principally on two issues: lowering the cost of living and reining in corruption. They should stick to those.

On the cost of living, they will vote early and often to end Trump’s tariff regime, either by disapproving existing ones or passing new legislation reclaiming congressional tariff authority. They will vote early and often on war powers resolutions to end the Iran war. They will vote to reverse Medicaid cuts—new work requirements for which will kick in next year—and Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program cuts, which have already kicked in. They’ll vote to restore enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies to lower health insurance premiums. In short, they’ll vote to reverse all of the MAGA moves that voters hated and that cost Republicans the election, leaving Republicans the choice to filibuster, veto, or sustain Trump’s veto on any of these popular moves.

Trickier tactical decisions will come on must-pass government-funding bills. Most notably, Democrats can use the power of the purse to cut off funding for the Iran war, and they’ll attempt something along those lines in their opening bids. But we can already see many of the new, novice Democratic members and senators from red states getting queasy when the question becomes whether to shut down the government over the issue, even though Democrats (and Republicans, for that matter) have heard pretty resoundingly from the voters that they want this war finished.

On corruption, there’s more to do beyond oversight hearings—and there will be oh so many of those. Because those hearings can and should fold into legislation. Among the many things we’re eager to learn more about is the level of insider trading, favor granting, and prediction-market gambling from within the White House. We suspect the findings will be substantial. And that’s a great opportunity to extend popular proposed bans on congressional stock trading to the White House, as well as to ban prediction-market betting in the executive branch.

As important as any individual policy, though, is the need to stick to them, and to stay focused squarely on what midterm voters demanded without getting sidetracked by factional demands from one segment of these big, broad majorities that put them at odds with the other. Democrats were handed a gift from God in these midterms that they didn’t actually deserve. The Democratic coalition had been in a death spiral, having comprehensively lost the white working-class vote and watching anxiously as minority working-class voters drifted in the same direction. Without some correction, the Democratic coalition would soon be down to English majors. Thanks to Trump doing everything in his power to shatter the very groups that got him elected, Democrats were able to earn a tryout in the Great Plains, in the Deep South, in Texas. If they want to stay a viable party in the Senate and the Electoral College, it’s imperative to show that they’ll stick to the program.

What we’re monitoring: How’s ol’ J.D. Vance going to wriggle his way out of this one?

Vice President J.D. Vance’s presidential hopes nosedived on Election Day, and he knows it. He’s the deputy to, and chief public cheerleader for, the very same president that the nation comprehensively rejected. And his legacy contribution to the midterm campaigns was to serve as chief public cheerleader for Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy after the candidate weaponized his opponent’s childhood rape against her. The 2028 presidential nomination has never looked more up for grabs.

So it wasn’t surprising that his damage control came quickly and at length in a Twitter essay the following morning. And it was our first look at how he would attempt to balance his day job with his need to separate himself from his day job.

“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote. “The president himself said so last night.” OK, sure, Trump admitted that energy prices were the factor. It gets more interesting in the next part. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” he added. “Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.”

To whom is this directed? He’s braying vaguely against neocons and hawks within the party. But he’s not allowed to be the avatar of the anti-war faction, as he’d like to be, because his boss started the war and made Vance a spokesperson for it. Maybe Trump will give him permission to become an open opponent of the war—he’s generally pretty loosey-goosey about demanding loyalty from his subjects, right? Right. Best of luck to Vance as he figures all this out!

He’s not the only presidential hopeful entering the essay contest. (It’s not a coincidence that these guys all have between one and two Ivy League diplomas.) Ted Cruz, now the lone statewide-elected Republican in the postrevolutionary Woke Texas, rattled off and gave credence to a whole list of voters’ concerns: “Food is too high, gas is too high, diesel is too high, insurance is too high, life is too high,” he wrote. “Tariffs have made everything too expensive, and the Iran war has dragged on too long.” He observes these things as if they just came out of the blue. Why are there tariffs? Why is there an Iran war? This man behind the curtain goes unnamed.

The game, then, is correctly blaming Trump’s policies for why the GOP crashed and burned, without ascribing those policy choices to a source.

What’s a bunch of nonsense that you should absolutely enjoy: Funny GOP excuses for why they lost.

For the 80th time: It’s not complicated why the GOP lost! Trump made things more expensive to amuse himself, while launching a losing war, while enriching himself, while being a jerk, while overplaying his hand on immigration enforcement, while building monuments to himself, while fighting hard to keep the Epstein files hidden, etc., etc. But let’s look at some of the other excuses out there.

Many of them come from Trump. He has argued that “Fox News bears responsibility for these losses by constantly and consistently putting on the Dumocrat opposition, and worse,” a thought that came to him while watching former New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio on the channel. We’d rank de Blasio’s persuasive abilities on cable news as relatively low on the reasons Republicans lost. Trump’s bigger argument is that Republicans lost because “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” It’s true Republicans get much better turnout among low-propensity GOP voters when Trump is on the ballot, or when it’s a presidential election cycle in general. But presidents are never on the ballot in the midterms—which come in the “middle” of a president’s “term”—and their party doesn’t typically lose the House popular vote by 14 points.

Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, a notable supporting figure in the administration’s collapse, posted: “We were too successful the first year of the Trump administration.” Ah, yes, the winning was all too front-loaded, cannibalizing wins that could have been had closer to election time. But Trump’s approval rating has been a downward line since Day 1.

Some right-wing commentators blamed the failure of Senate Republicans to pass the SAVE America Act, the GOP’s strict voter-ID and voter-verification law, for the losses. And, sure, maybe its burdensome requirements could have disenfranchised some new registrants from exercising their right to vote. But can we now finally finish talking about the need for the SAVE America Act? Here are some of the states with the strictest voter-ID requirements and, in parentheses, how the GOP fared in those states: Indiana (yikes), Ohio (yikes), Mississippi (yikes), Georgia (yikes), North Carolina (YIKES). What that also does show, on the other hand, is that Democrats have an opportunity, should they want to ever attempt a bipartisan election-reform bill, to compromise with Republicans on a form of national voter ID without being so

More plunder …

• We feel as if we’ve read less articles and seen fewer questions about whether Trump will “moderate” after the midterms or “change” in some way after seeing the nation’s verdict. Everyone simply knows he won’t. And Trump made his intentions especially clear on Friday, when he announced that he was replacing chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller, the architect and executor of various policies—especially the immigration-related ones—that led to Tuesday’s wipeout. On the other hand, he’s a pretty accomplished guy: He was able to turn Texas blue, after all.

• A unifying position among Democrats across the political spectrum this fall was that they should impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the erstwhile weekend-cable-news co-host who pushed for and did not win the Iran war while firing and/or alienating all the competent people around him. But Democrats may not get the chance next year, because it may happen next week. When the House reconvenes, Republican Rep. Thomas Massie will force a vote on Hegseth’s impeachment. All, or nearly all, Democrats will support it. But how many Republicans will? We’d expect a lot of interest. A great many House Republicans lost their seats because of this guy and now have to come back for a lame-duck session. Would you be in a “Let’s vote to save Pete Hegseth” kind of mood while you were cleaning out your office after losing an R +15 district? They might as well try to do it by unanimous consent. Hegseth sure seems to be preparing for a trial.

• Democrats may be on the verge of flipping nine Senate seats. Let’s chastise them for not getting more! There are two glaring missed opportunities on the map. Republican Julia Letlow won the Louisiana Senate race by only 1.8 points against Democrat Jamie Davis. This race had similar characteristics to Mississippi and South Carolina: stunningly high Black voter turnout after the Supreme Court’s latest whack at the Voting Rights Act, and a ho-hum Republican candidate with no competitive general-election experience. Perhaps Senate Democrats’ super PAC could’ve thrown a couple million bucks its way. And in Montana, the opposition to Republican Kurt Alme was split between Democrat Alani Bankhead and independent Seth Bodnar, when Bodnar should’ve just cut it with the cutesiness and beat Bankhead in the Democratic primary. He probably would have won. Maybe in the next rare historic tsunami with no modern comparison!

• There’s always one drop early on election night that tells you where things are going. In 2020, Joe Biden’s underwhelming early vote margin in Miami-Dade County suggested that there was going to be a massive polling error that year. In 2024, it was Kamala Harris’ underperformance in Loudoun County, Virginia. This year, it was the wildly terrible early vote numbers for Victoria Spartz in Indiana’s 5th District. Spartz ended up losing her “likely Republican”–rated seat, while other Indiana Republicans held on. The only reason those other Indiana Republicans may have held on, though, is because state Republicans resisted ferocious pressure from the administration, and Speaker Mike Johnson, to maximally gerrymander their state. Trump punished those reluctant state senators by successfully primarying them out of office. In the end, their sacrifice may have been the only thing that prevented a wipeout of the whole delegation.

• Elections aren’t always one-sided disasters, so let’s look at all the Democratic seats that Republicans flipped in the House. They flipped Tennessee’s 9th District, which state Republicans had gerrymandered into a Trump +21 seat, by a single point. They won one (1) of the five Texas districts they attempted to gerrymander Democrats out of: Texas’ 32nd. And last but not least, former Maine Gov. Paul LePage won Maine’s 2nd District. He certainly benefited from the performance of Susan Collins, who, even in losing, was the only Senate candidate to improve upon Republicans’ statewide margin relative to 2024. Anyway, that’s the whole list as of this writing. And LePage’s district, which Trump won by 9 in 2024, appears to be the bluest seat held by a Republican. Tsunamis (electoral) are nuts!

• After having bequeathed the lousy Democrats the largest House majority for either party this century, Johnson declared his work complete and announced he wouldn’t stay on as House Republican leader to lead a hollowed-out conference that will have no relevance whatsoever for the next two years. The race to succeed him appears to be between Reps. Jim Jordan and Steve Scalise. Our first thought is: Who gives a shit? Our second thought is: See first thought.
news.summary: Plus: How do Democrats surf their giant blue wave without wiping out completely?
news.author: Jim Newell

news.title: Young voters, including men, swung dramatically back towards Democrats
news.text:
Republicans' 2024 gains among young voters were reversed in the midterms, as voters under 30 overwhelmingly preferred Democratic congressional candidates.

Seventy-three percent of voters under 30 cast ballots for Democratic midterm candidates for the House of Representatives, and young men swung back to Democrats, according to exit polls from the Nov. 3 election. Only 25% of young voters cast ballots for Republican candidates.

Democrats won 62% of voters ages 30-44 and 52% of those 45-64. Republicans' strongest age group was Americans 65 and over, who split their votes precisely 50-50 between the two parties.

In 2024, 54% of the young voters favored Vice President Kamala Harris and 43% of them voted for President Donald Trump. In 2018, the last time Democrats enjoyed a strong midterm election, 68% of young voters cast ballots for Democrats in the House.

"I didn't think I would see another set of numbers that were so favorable to Democrats (as) in 2018 ever again," Director of Polling John Della Volpe, of the Harvard Youth Poll, who has studied young voters since 2000, told USA TODAY.

Della Volpe noted that final 2026 election numbers are still incomplete but "if those numbers hold in this cycle, it would have matched or exceeded that number," adding, "That is striking."

A swing from Trump to Democrats

A vote analysis from Tufts University's Center for Information and Research on Civic Learning and Engagement (CIRCLE) found that 15% of young people who voted for Trump in 2024 voted for a Democratic House candidate in the midterms. 

CIRCLE noted on a press call that the Nov. 5 report was its first public estimates. The organization plans to release more precise data in months ahead, after all of the election voter reports are complete.

However, the change in young voters' partisan preference may also be a reflection of 2024 voters who stayed home this cycle and new 2026 voters who turned out.

"Shifts among demographic groups don't necessarily mean that young voters changed their minds. It can reflect who showed up versus who stayed home, and young people who are new to the electorate can produce that same aggregate shift," Newhouse Director Leela Strong, of Tufts University's CIRCLE, said on a Nov. 5 press call. 

Della Volpe said it will be some time before the data is able to explain that, but he speculated it was a different group of voters than in 2024.

"I think it will probably take some time before the data science and the voter file people kind of collect the data to figure that out. However, it was likely a different composition," Della Volpe said.

Data from The New York Times' Voter Trends notes that voters ages 18-29 had a 33-point swing to Democrats, when compared with 2024 votes for Harris, while voters 30-44 had a 24-point swing to Democrats. Voters ages 45-64 had a 13-point swing and voters 65 and older had a 6-point swing.

In 2024, young men swung towards Trump and played a role in sending him back to the White House. In 2024, 49% of young men voted for Trump and 48% voted for Harris. 

But in the midterms, young men swung back to Democrats. Polling ahead of the election indicated that the young male group preferred Democrats and exit polling found 66% of males 18-29 years old voted Democratic.

Della Volpe told USA TODAY in October that "a vote for Donald Trump did not mean that younger people or younger men were signing up to be Republicans for life." 

Strong said that in addition to young men, young rural voters and young people without any college experience also swung back to Democrats. CIRCLE, which studies young people's civic engagement and political participation, also reported that the economy was a top concern for the young voter cohort. 

Della Volpe told USA TODAY that he wasn't necessarily surprised by the overwhelming Democratic support by young voters because in the most recent Harvard Youth Poll, his researchers found that only 9% of young voters thought the country was headed in the right direction.

"We certainly saw all the underlying factors that led to this," he said. "At the end of the day, younger men in particular responded to a series of what they considered to be broken promises."

Della Volpe previously told USA TODAY that in his focus groups in 2024, young voters told him they were voting based on the economy. In 2026, the Harvard Youth Poll found that, two years into the Republican administration, economic concerns still plagued young voters.

More: New poll reveals where young voters stand as midterms near

Low youth turnout

Young people represented about 11% of the electorate, and the young voter turnout rate landed at 27%, according to estimates by CIRCLE, which is 4 points lower than the group's record-high 31% participation in the 2018 midterms. 

A separate estimate from the U.S. Census Bureau, though, says that 36% of 18-29 year olds voted in 2018.

Regardless, this year's 27% turnout for young voters is high when compared with the group historically voting at a rate between 15% to 20% in midterms.

Exit polls said that while young voters made up 11% of the electorate, 20% came from voters 30-44 years old, 34% from voters 45-64 and 36% from voters 65 and older.

Strong said that this third consecutive midterm cycle of young voter turnout above 27% suggests young voters have become more engaged in politics.

"It tells us that young people are sending a clear signal that they want to take action and drive change, and that this is no longer just an anomaly around a single election," Strong said. "It is closer to a repeatable feature in the midterm electorate."

news.title: How Republicans Got Swept Away by the Blue Tsunami in Six Charts
news.text: Two years after carrying President Donald Trump and Republicans to power, the GOP coalition appeared to come apart. Men backed Democratic House candidates 50 percent to 48 percent in the poll, conducted by SSRS for major news organizations. It was the first time Democrats carried men in the national House vote since 2008, according to a Newsweek review of exit polls. Democrats won men under 30 by 35 points. White women, a group Republicans won by 11 points in the 2024 House vote, backed Democrats by 6. The GOP also lost Latino men, who swung 27 points toward Democrats, and its 13-point lead with voters without college degrees shrank to 2. Meanwhile, white voters without degrees stayed with Republicans, though by smaller margins, and rural voters backed the party 57 percent to 41 percent. White evangelicals barely moved. The result was a Democratic majority in the House as well as in the Senate where Democrats will hold at least 54 seats after flipping seven held by Republicans in Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas. They could still win two more, in Alaska and in Mississippi. In the House, Democrats will have at least 253 House seats, including 43 pickups, with 21 races still to be called as of Friday afternoon, according to Associated Press projections. In The AP Voter Poll, 44 percent of voters said their House ballot was to express opposition to Trump. About two-thirds of voters said Trump's policies had "worsened economic conditions in the U.S." . And roughly a third called the Iran war a "crucial" factor in their vote for Congress. "What we saw was a massive rebuke of Donald Trump and a rejection of the Republican Party that's been enabling him," Mike Madrid, a Republican strategist who studies the Latino vote, told Newsweek. The charts compare House votes in the 2024 exit poll and the 2026 AP Voter Poll, not Trump’s 2024 race against former Vice President Kamala Harris. Turnout is usually lower in midterms, so the electorates differ. Different methods and different electorates mean the shifts are estimates. The latter survey of about 79,500 respondents was conducted by SSRS between October 19 and November 3. The margin of error was plus or minus 0.6 percentage points. Margins, or shifts toward Democrats, below are calculated by subtracting the Republican share from the Democratic share. How Latino Voting Shifted Latino voters backed Democratic House candidates by 9 points in 2024. This year, the margin was 30. Latino men favored Republicans by 8 points in the 2024 House vote and Democrats by 19 on Tuesday, a 27-point swing. Latinos under 30 moved 50 points toward Democrats, though that subgroup is small. “You saw in 2024, all the Latino communities moved to the right,” Mike Madrid said, and “in 2026, all of the Latino communities moved to the left.” Older Latinos went the other way however. Those 65 and older backed Democrats by 10 points, down from 16 in 2024. Maria Cardona, a Democratic strategist, told Newsweek that Republicans “made a massive miscalculation” by treating their 2024 numbers as a permanent realignment. “The Latino vote swung back to the Democrats but it will be temporary if the Democrats can’t make a policy impact for them,” Brandon Rottinghaus, a political science professor at the University of Houston, told Newsweek. How Young Male Voting Shifted Young men were a key part of Trump's 2024 coalition and many experts still considered them a key swing vote for the current race. On Tuesday, men under 30 backed Democrats 66 percent to 31 percent, a 35-point margin. That margin was +3 points in the 2024 House vote. Women under 30 favored Democrats by 24 points in the 2024 House vote. This year, they did so by 57 points, a 33-point shift. Men as a whole went from a 14-point Republican advantage to a 2-point Democratic edge, 50 percent to 48 percent, the first time Democrats won men in the national House vote since 2008, according to a Newsweek review of exit polls. White men moved 17 points toward Democrats, and Black men moved 23. About one in 10 Black men backed the Republican in their House race, according to the poll. Republican hopefuls will have to pursue 2024 Trump voters who defected this year, “especially young white men, Latino voters, and working-class voters,” Asher Hildebrand, a professor at Duke University’s Sanford School of Public Policy, told Newsweek. “They will also need to address these voters’ economic anxieties and improve their quality of life,” he said. How Non-College Educated Americans Voted Voters without college degrees have anchored Trump's party for a decade. They still preferred Republicans on Tuesday, 50 percent to 48 percent, but the 13-point margin of 2024 shrank to 2—an 11-point shift. But the education divide still widened in 2026 as college graduates moved even further toward Democrats by a 28-point margin, 17 points more than in 2024. White voters without degrees remained the party's strongest demographic base. White men in that group backed Republicans by 28 points, and white women by 16. White Women Crossed Over White women made up 38 percent of the 2026 electorate in the Voter Poll, the largest group in the gender-by-race breakdown. They voted 52 percent to 46 percent for Democrats after backing Republicans by 11 points in the 2024 House vote, a 17-point shift. The move toward Democrats occurred on both sides of the education divide. White women with degrees backed Democrats by 29 points, up from 13 in 2024, a 16-point shift. Those without degrees still backed Republicans, by 16 points, down from 30, a 14-point shift. Catholics Shifted Toward Democrats Catholics backed Republicans by 21 points in the 2024 House vote. This year, they split almost evenly, 50 percent to 49 percent for Democrats, a 22-point swing. White Catholics still favored Republicans—56 percent to 43 percent— a 13-point margin that is 16 points fewer than in 2024. Voters with no religion moved 16 points toward Democrats. Jewish voters moved the other way. They still backed Democrats 68 percent to 31 percent, a 37-point margin, though less than in 2024 when that margin was 50 points. White evangelicals backed Republicans 82 percent to 16 percent, a 4-point change, though they fell to 17 percent of the electorate from 23 percent in the 2024 exit poll. How Far Rural Voters Moved Rural and small-town voters stayed with Republicans on Tuesday, 57 percent to 41 percent. The Voter Poll changed how it asks voters where they live in 2026, so those figures can’t be directly compared with 2024. Democrats still won in rural states. Adam Hamilton’s win in Kansas made him the first Democrat to win a Senate seat there since 1932. “This year has been one of the worst farming years of my 43 year career,” John Boyd Jr., founder of the National Black Farmers Association, told Newsweek on Thursday. “Many white farmers were so upset with Trump they stayed home, which is why you saw such a huge difference in rural America,” he said. Black farmers, he added, were voting early. Derrell Peel, an agricultural economist at Oklahoma State University who stressed he is not a political analyst, called the vote “a reaction to what we’ve been through.” “It’s certainly temporary for now, but could it have permanent impacts? I think it’s possible that it could,” he told Newsweek. 'Register Their Displeasure With Trump' Among voters who said they backed Trump two years ago, 91 percent chose Republican House candidates on Tuesday. Seven percent went to Democrats. Trump won the popular vote in 2024, yet House voters who said they backed Harris outnumbered those who said they backed Trump in this year’s electorate, 49 percent to 44 percent. People who said they sat out the 2024 presidential race (4 percent of voters) broke for Democrats, 70 percent to 25 percent. Trump was on many voters’ minds. Forty-four percent said they cast a House ballot to oppose him and 16 percent to support him, with his approval at 37 percent. Voters who called the cost of living crucial, 49 percent of voters, favored Democrats 66 percent to 32 percent. Democrats did not come out of it popular. Fifty-two percent of voters viewed the party unfavorably, against 47 percent who viewed it favorably. “Nothing here could be inferred as an affirmation of the Democratic Party,” Madrid said. “Put simply, voters dislike President Trump but still do not trust Democrats,” Doug Gordon, a Democratic strategist with Upshift Strategies, told Newsweek. “The midterm wins are borrowed time from voters who wanted to register their displeasure with Trump.”
news.summary: House polls show that voters who backed Donald Trump's GOP in 2024 swung toward Democrats in 2026.
news.author: Jesus Mesa

news.title: ‘Finally there’s hope’: UK weighs up opportunities and risks after Trump’s midterms disaster
news.text:
Andy Burnham was having dinner at the Commonwealth summit in Antigua when the results of the US midterm elections started rolling in.

UK government officials in the Caribbean with the prime minister scrolled through their phones with growing incredulity as the scale of the Republicans’ defeat became clear.

“We knew it was going to be bad for Trump but it was historic result after historic result: Kansas, South Carolina, Texas,” one said. “We’ve been dealing with this constant anxiety over Trump’s erraticism and what he might do next for years. Finally, there’s a bit of hope.”

As he faced the cameras the following morning, Burnham struggled to disguise his relief that the US president could be restrained.

“I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all and that’s the cost of living,” he said. “But I can’t get people’s cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved … I’ll be working for de-escalation, to make it very clear.”

Burnham will not be alone in urging restraint. The energy price shock and subsequent interest rate hikes caused by the US war on Iran have severely affected economies around the world.

It is the main reason why this set of midterm elections – in which the Democrats took control of Congress – are the most consequential for the UK in decades, with the potential to have a greater impact at home than almost any domestic announcement.

Earlier this month, the prime minister admitted his first budget had been “less radical than he had hoped”, with the global economic volatility forcing the government’s hand.

But while the trajectory of the Iran conflict is the inevitable focus, it is not the only direct impact of the Republican rout on the UK. Trump’s potential approach to Russia and Ukraine, the threat of more tariffs and the wider political ripples of the “blue tsunami” are all being pored over at Westminster.

While the US president’s domestic powers will be constrained, he still wields significant influence over foreign policy – and is likely to use it.

“We’ve all learned over recent years that all of this lands on the desk of just one decision-maker in Washington. How he interprets these elections matters more than how they’re seen in any other global capital,” one UK government insider said.

Yet there are expectations that Trump could still be curtailed by a Democratic-run Congress trying to push the party’s domestic agenda while also holding the Trump court to account and using up all his spare bandwidth.

“Congress probably will become a thorn in the president’s side, so he may become distracted by those issues rather than international ones,” said Sarah Elliott, the director of the special relationship unit at the Prosperity Institute.

David Miliband, a former UK foreign secretary now based in New York, said: “There is a chance that the cross-party congressional majority to support Ukraine finds its voice and leverage. I hope so.

“Maybe the impact of tariffs on prices will prompt a second look. But the presidency remains ‘imperial’ in foreign policy, so there are no guarantees.”

Kim Darroch, the UK’s man in Washington the last time Trump was in office, said the president still had the ability to wreak chaos on the world stage.

“You can’t formally declare war without congressional approval but you can engage in conflict. He can impose tariffs and insult allies and cosy up to dictators. All of that is still open to Trump,” he said.

“My instinct is that he’s held his views about the uselessness of allies, the value of tariffs, the world being about bigger powers for decades. He’s not going to change his mind now.”

However, over the past few days, the mood music in Washington toward Iran already appears to have shifted. There is hope in diplomatic circles that the midterms have strengthened the resolve in Washington for a negotiated conclusion to the war.

Miliband said: “I would guess that the odds on renewed assault on Iran have lengthened, and the pressure for resolution will be strengthened.”

Others, however, are more cautious, warning that Trump, who appeared to agree with JD Vance’s post-result assessment that the war was to blame, had a record of unpredictability.

Emily Thornberry, the chair of the Commons foreign affairs committee, said: “Equally likely – and that’s the problem – is that he might use his three aircraft carriers and his buildup of troops in the Gulf and just decide he’s going to invade. Honestly, we don’t know.”

Lord Darroch said: “Trump could go for one last massive attack, particularly focusing on blowing up nuclear sites. Then he could walk away and be able to say it’s been obliterated – again.”

UK ministers are, however, cautiously optimistic. The markets appear to be as well – with oil prices dropping sharply after the results.

“We know all the risks. We know he could change his mind on Iran again, that he could strike a deal with Putin that locks out Ukraine, that he could announce more indiscriminate tariffs,” one minister said. “But we also see this as a moment of opportunity.”

Thornberry highlighted the Democrats’ very different foreign policy agenda. “Let’s see what happens. I think they come in from January and believe that they’ve got a mandate to finish the Iranian war,” she said.

“On top of that, they are much more sympathetic, as is the general public, to the plight of the Ukrainians and believe that the American president is not playing fair.”

Labour figures are already building links in the new-look Congress, with some Democrats proposing a bill modelled on Labour’s approach to Israeli settlers in the West Bank.

UK ministers say they have had no indications that Trump is planning more tariffs – though acknowledge they could be taken by surprise. “If the UK does something big on legislation or regulation surrounding big tech or AI, then you can imagine it happening,” one said.

But some in UK policy circles argue that a Democrat-run Congress could help advance some of the UK’s international priorities, such as AI regulation or clean energy, both of which have been resisted by the Trump White House.

Government sources said that while they would revive traditional links between Labour and the Democrats before the next presidential election, they were proceeding carefully.

More than one cited the fact that Trump accused Labour of “interference” during the last presidential election after party staff volunteered for Kamala Harris’s campaign. “We need to be cautious – but also it’s entirely reasonable for us to engage with them,” a senior aide said.

Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, met Gavin Newsom, the California governor and a presidential hopeful, last year. But he also attended a college football game in Atlanta with his counterpart, Marco Rubio.

Others inside Labour – including at cabinet level – already have close ties with Democratic allies. Party strategists will reflect on the midterm election tactics, with a view to adopting parts that could work against their opponents on the populist right.

Labour MPs may be relieved that American voters have cast their verdict on Trump and his combative style of politics, with the US just the latest in a list of countries that have rejected rightwing populism at the ballot box.

But party strategists warn against assuming Reform UK would necessarily suffer the same fate. “It’s all about the cost of living: unless we show that we have the answers voters could still look elsewhere,” one said.

Republicans also deny the era is over. Elliott said: “As long as immigration is on the rise and there is poor assimilation of immigrants in western countries, rightwing populism will be a force in politics.”

Senior Labour figures have cautioned against looking too celebratory over the results. “It wasn’t a ringing endorsement of the Dems, just like the last election here wasn’t about an outpouring of affection for Keir,” they said.

“In both cases it was about giving the incumbent a kicking, and all of us progressives need to be careful not to take the wrong message from it.”

UK officials insist it is business as usual as far as Trump is concerned. “It’s important we show respect for the fact that his administration has two years to go,” one said.

Darroch cautioned British politicians against prematurely – or too overtly – focusing on Trump’s potential successors.

“Burnham has to be careful he doesn’t appear to be moving on from Trump and dismissing him as a spent force,” he added. “He will be there until the end. Trump will not gallop gently into a golden sunset. He will rage against the weakening of his grip on power.”
news.summary:
Senior British politicians and officials highlight potential to end Iran war but warn US president is not yet ‘a spent force’

Andy Burnham was having dinner at the Commonwealth summit in Antigua when the results of the US midterm elections started rolling in.

UK government officials in the Caribbean with the prime minister scrolled through their phones with growing incredulity as the scale of the Republicans’ defeat became clear.

news.title: New pope, rise of Luke Littler and what that has happened since Spurs last won four games in a row
news.text:
It has been 1,108 days since Tottenham last won four Premier League games in a row - a run they could end this weekend when they face Leeds at Elland Road.

Not since the opening months of Ange Postecoglou’s reign have Spurs won more than three times in succession - a feat they quickly achieved twice either side of a north London derby draw under the Australian between August and October 2023 - and a lot has happened in the intervening three years.

That season, fast-starting Tottenham won eight of their first 10 fixtures and went five points clear at the summit despite the high-profile summer loss of Harry Kane to Bayern Munich, eventually finishing in fifth place.

Here, Standard Sport looks at some of the biggest stories to have happened since Spurs last won four on the bounce.

Cardinal Robert Francis Prevost was elected as the 267th Pope of the Catholic Church in May 2025, taking the name Pope Leo XIV.

While Pope Leo is said to be a Real Madrid fan, he was gifted a Sunderland shirt with the name "Pope Leo, 14" emblazoned on the back ahead of the club’s Europa League campaign.

Pope Leo was gifted the shirt after Sunderland’s chaplain, Father Marc Lyden-Smith, gave one to Pope Francis ahead of the Black Cats’ victory over Newcastle in 2013.

Donald Trump was re-elected as President of the United States in November 2024, defeating Democratic candidate and former vice-president Kamala Harris.

It came four years after Mr Trump had lost the 2020 election to Joe Biden, ending his initial spell in the White House after victory over Hillary Clinton in 2016.

The Labour Party came back into power after 14 years as Sir Keir Starmer was elected as UK Prime Minister in July 2024.

Despite a landslide victory, Starmer resigned in July 2026 and was replaced by Andy Burnham.

The UK has now had five Prime Ministers in the last five years.

Daniel Levy stepped down as executive chairman of Tottenham in September 2025, bringing to an end his 25-year reign at the club.

Following Levy’s departure, non-executive chairman Peter Charrington declared “a new era of leadership for the club” before Spurs went on to endure their worst season in Premier League history as they only narrowly avoided relegation to the Championship on the final day.

Tottenham would have been relegated had they not mustered up a nervy 1-0 win at home to Everton on the final day of last season.

12 months after lifting the Europa League, their first major trophy for 17 years, Spurs would remarkably become mired in a relegation battle with rivals West Ham, staying up by the skin of their teeth thanks to a goal from loanee Joao Palhinha.

Spurs’ decision to get rid of Postecoglou just 16 days after he guided them to Europa League success over Manchester United in Bilbao was always going to prove controversial.

No one, though, could have foreseen the disaster that would unfurl over the next season as Tottenham went through three managerial changes in 10 months.

Thomas Frank was brought in as Postecoglou’s successor, but was eventually sacked in February 2026 with the club hovering over the relegation zone.

His replacement, Igor Tudor, lasted just 44 days before the club hit the panic button again to bring in Roberto De Zerbi to steer them to safety.

In the space of three years, West Ham went from Conference League winners to being relegated to the Championship.

A series of poor recruitment decisions, managerial changes and ownership uncertainty ensured the Hammers failed to build on their first piece of major silverware in 43 years before eventually dropping back to the second tier after 14 seasons.

Darts sensation Luke Littler announced himself on the biggest stage at just 16 years old as he made a historic run to the World Championship final on his debut at Alexandra Palace in January 2024.

Since then, Littler has become a back-to-back world champion and underlined his place as the best player on the planet while still a teenager.

Another sporting prodigy, Kimi Antonelli has risen from obscurity to the top of his sport in the last three years.

At just 20 years and 68 days old, Kimi Antonelli became the youngest Formula One world champion in history on Sunday after clinching the 2026 title with a third-place finish at the Mexico City Grand Prix.

A record-breaking campaign has also seen Antonelli become the youngest winner of the Monaco Grand Prix, the youngest driver to achieve a Grand Slam, and the first Italian in more than 60 years to be crowned world champion.

Sir Andy Murray and Rafael Nadal retired within a few months of each other to leave Novak Djokovic as the last man standing from the ‘Big Four’ era of 21st century tennis.

Two-time Wimbledon winner Murray retired in August 2024 and was swiftly followed by 22-time Grand Slam champion Nadal in October. It followed Roger Federer’s retirement in September 2022.

Boxing fans have long since grown weary of Tyson Fury’s retirement U-turns, so his fourth announcement last year that he was hanging up his gloves convinced few. Just a handful of months later, he made the decision to step back into the ring for a fifth, and surely, final time in April 2026.

The former world heavyweight champion beat Russian Arslanbek Makhmudov by unanimous decision in his first fight back and is now gearing up for a hotly-anticipated bout with Anthony Joshua in Cardiff in December, having also defeated Mariusz Wach in Thailand.
news.summary: It has been over three years since Spurs won four Premier League games in a row

news.title: 'Dirty' Trump deserved to be thrashed in the US midterms, says Kemi Badenoch
news.text:
Kemi Badenoch says Donald Trump 'deserved to be thrashed' in the US elections and has denounced his 'dirty' style of politics.

In a sweeping attack on the American President's record she criticised him over the Iran War, for threatening Canada and Greenland, imposing swingeing tariffs and “squabbling with allies” like the UK.

Trump's heavy defeat in the US mid term elections was “entirely self inflicted”, she told The Independent Editor-in-Chief Geordie Greig.

Controversially, Badenoch said she would have been content if Trump had never won a second term in the White House and his Democrat opponent, Left winger Kamala Harris had become President in 2024 instead.

In the wide-ranging exclusive interview for The Talk Show, Badenoch also savaged Tory predecessors Boris Johnson and Liz Truss for their “mistakes” in government.

She said Andy Burnham was more “fun” than Keir Starmer, but behind the “charm” he was “dangerous.”

She called Nigel Farage's Reform Party “bonkers” and ruled out serving in a Conservative-Reform Coalition led by him.

But she conceded that before his dip in popularity, Farage had made an “emotional connection” with voters that the Tories had lost until she became leader.

Badenoch's outspoken condemnation of Trump's policies and personality may come as a surprise, especially to Tory supporters, some of whom urged her to copy him after he won power. 

Asked if he deserved to be thrashed, she did not hesitate: “Yeah. He has not been acting in the way that I would consider conservative. Where is the push for free markets and better trade... rather than protectionism, America first, the squabbling with allies? That's not what conservatives do.

“Trump is very charming in person, but you see the way that he talks about journalists, about individuals. It doesn't meet the standards a statesman should meet - always wanting to get dirty in terms of insults and and so on.

“When he was rude about Keir Starmer... I didn't like that at all. What they did to President Zelensky in the White House was awful.”

Trump had won power “with an extraordinary coalition of Latinos, more Black voters than any other Republican” - and wasted it. 

“What's the first thing he does? Tariffs, and then talking about Greenland and Canada. A lot of people were wondering, ‘what are you doing?’”

She understood Trump's initial decision to go to war with Iran - which she had backed. 

“We don't want them getting nuclear weapons. But where's the plan?”

Join us as an Independent member and support our journalism for just £1 . Sign up here

His defeat in the mid term elections was “entirely self-inflicted”, she said. “Voters want results.”

Ms Badenoch claimed she would have been happy if Trump had lost the last presidential election - and revealed a hitherto unknown admiration for fellow black female politician Kamala Harris.

“People ask me who did I prefer, Kamala Harris, Donald Trump? I would say I like them both equally. Make of that what you will.”

While refusing to 'name and blame' former Conservative PMs Johnson and Truss, she was fiercely critical of both their records in No 10. They were guilty of “gimmicks, mistakes and short termism. Everybody made mistakes. Obviously, the leaders were responsible for most of them. Immigration was too high.”

Did she mean Johnson and the so called 'Boris wave' of immigration? 

“People know who the prime minister was then,” she said, removing all doubt.

Truss got equally short shrift. Badenoch savaged the disastrous budget that saw Truss kicked out of Downing Street after six weeks.

“You can't just announce £150 billion bailing out people's energy bills and £45 billion of tax cuts with no spending cuts at all,” she said disbelievingly. 

“Those are the wrong way of doing things.”

Rather than call out Johnson and Truss personally, Badenoch, a Methodist, quoted St Augustine: “Hate the sin, love the sinner.”

She deflected the notion that Burnham's “charm” has revived Labour fortunes since awkward Starmer's demise.

Calling him a “foot in mouth” politician, she says: “He says things first and then thinks about it later.”

He is more genial. I'm not sure I would call it charm. He looks like he'd be more fun company at a party, (but) that makes him more dangerous because he wants to please everybody.”

With the latest polls indicating the Conservatives have narrowed the gap with Labour to two points, she insists she has his measure, boasting: “The more Andy Burnham sees of me, the less he wants to have an early election.”

She is equally confident about seeing off the challenge from Farage, whose ratings have fallen in the wake of a series of scandals to hit him and Reform. It has coincided with the Conservatives overtaking Reform in the political ratings war.

“At the moment, I am beating him, and I think he's very worried about that.”

She freely admitted Farage initially struck a chord with the public at a time the Tories were floundering. 

“What worked for him was having an emotional connection and an authenticity which we as a party had lost, sounding very technocratic.”

That had all changed now she was Tory leader and the shine was coming off Farage. 

“One of the things going wrong for him was that he pretended to be this everyman. 

“A lot of his supporters... don't understand how he's getting £5 million and they're not able to pay their energy bills.”

It was up to a Commons inquiry to decide if Farage's £5 million donation from a crypto currency billionaire was “corrupt”, said Badenoch. But she has made up her mind. 

“His story doesn't add up.”

She is just as adamant she would never serve under 'Prime Minister Farage.'

“No, because he would not be good for this country. I simply wouldn't.”

Some of Reform's ideas, such as a recent proposal to ‘nationalise Poundland' were plain “bonkers”.

She claimed Farage did her a favour with the acrimonious defection of defeated Tory leadership rival Robert Jenrick to Reform earlier this year.

Getting rid of Jenrick was like defusing an “unexploded bomb” - leaks from the Shadow Cabinet ceased overnight, she said.

Badenoch joked: “The only thing I haven't done is written a thank you card to Nigel Farage for taking these problems away. I'll write it in his Christmas card!”

She defended her aggressive style at the Commons despatch box.

“You have to be a fighter to survive. There are 400 Labour MPs screaming and shouting. I need to put some of those people in their place. It's a kill or be killed arena.”

Which explains why she refused to say sorry for calling ex Education Secretary Bridget Phillipson “spiteful” for the closure of private schools as a result of Labour's VAT on school fees. 

“Spiteful. What's wrong with that?” she retorted.

“She hurt many, many children. They had to leave their schools, which closed down. It was class war. So yes, I will call it like it is.

“We've spent a lot of time dressing things up in fancy words where most of the public don't understand what we're talking about.”

After putting a difficult start as Conservative leader behind her, Ms Badenoch said Labour and Reform jibes do not get under her thick skin. Even if they did she would not show it.

She is proud of being a 'cool customer,' adding: “I'm a poker player. I have a very good poker face.

“I remember saying to some people I get better every day, and they mocked it. But it's true. I believe in continuous improvement.”
news.summary: In a wide-ranging and revealing exclusive interview for The Talk Show with Geordie Greig, Badenoch also savaged Tory predecessors Boris Johnson and Liz Truss for their ‘mistakes’ in government
